domains.name: Cohesion & Coherence
domains.summary: This domain covers the resources that make a text hang together for its reader: cohesive ties (reference, conjunction, lexical cohesion) and the information-structuring choices (given–new order, thematic progression, encapsulation, text patterns) that make a sequence of sentences read as a purposeful whole. It treats cohesion as a means to coherence rather than a proxy for it, countering the connector-heavy, checklist approach that learner-corpus findings and test preparation tend to reinforce. Topics move from sentence-to-sentence linking towards text-level signalling and the reader-oriented expectations of English-medium academic writing, including spoken signposting in lectures and presentations.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how writers and speakers help their audience follow their thinking — by linking sentences, keeping key terms consistent, putting familiar information first and signalling where a text is going — and why adding more linking words does not by itself make writing clear.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes concentrate on basic connectors, pronoun and noun reference, paragraph-level patterns and signposting in lectures, using short model texts and subject textbooks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses move learners from connector lists to information flow, encapsulation and reverse outlining for coherence in extended source-based writing.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional work diagnoses coherence problems in students' own assignments, especially reliance on connectors, unclear reference and weak transitions between paragraphs.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on dissertation-length coherence, terminological consistency and transitions between sections, and on using text patterns to read efficiently.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine flow in dense prose (thematic progression, encapsulation) and manage metatext and terminology across a thesis or article.

domains.name: Rhetorical Functions
domains.summary: This domain covers recurrent rhetorical functions — defining, classifying, describing processes and structures, comparing, expressing cause and effect, exemplifying, explaining, hypothesising, recommending, summarising, narrating and evaluating — that cut across genres and disciplines. It follows the discourse approach to English for science and technology (Trimble), Mohan's knowledge framework and functional genre work (Martin and Rose; Nesi and Gardner's genre families), treating each function as a pairing of a communicative purpose with characteristic lexicogrammar and organisation. Functions are building blocks for paragraphs, sections and whole genres; teaching them through authentic disciplinary exemplars rather than decontextualised phrase lists keeps the focus on what each function achieves.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the common jobs that academic texts do — such as defining a term, comparing two approaches, explaining why something happens or recommending action — and the language and organisation that each job typically needs.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes teach the core functions (defining, classifying, describing processes, comparing, cause and effect, exemplifying) through subject content, often in science, engineering and business contexts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses combine functions within extended assignments, focusing on explaining, evaluating, problem–solution and recommending in source-based writing.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support targets the functions demanded by specific assignments and genre families, such as explanation, critique and case study.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support emphasises contested and operational definitions, criterion-based evaluation, explanation of results and recommendations in dissertations and reports.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers mainly revisit hypothesising, defining contested constructs and explaining results within research genres.

domains.name: Stance, Metadiscourse & Evaluation
domains.summary: This domain covers the interpersonal dimension of academic discourse: how writers and speakers signal certainty and commitment, evaluate ideas and sources, represent themselves, engage readers, and keep their own claims distinct from those they attribute to others. It draws on Hyland's models of metadiscourse and of stance and engagement and on Martin and White's appraisal framework, especially engagement, treating them as complementary lenses rather than a single taxonomy. Stance is approached as calibration and positioning grounded in evidence, not as lists of hedges to insert, and disciplinary variation is made explicit throughout.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to show how sure you are about a claim and how to evaluate other people's work fairly. You will also learn when and how to make your own voice heard, and how to show the reader which ideas are yours and which come from your sources.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes introduce basic hedging and boosting, qualified generalisations and simple opinion language in speech and writing, linked to avoiding sweeping claims.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Pre-sessional courses develop calibration of claims to evidence, the averral–attribution distinction in source-based writing, concession, and informed choices about self-mention.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support helps students build an authorial voice in assignments, evaluate sources rather than describe them, and match stance conventions to their discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on critical evaluation of literature, dialogic positioning in literature reviews and calibrated claims in dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine stance for publication: claiming contribution without over-claiming, positioning against the literature, managing self-mention and engaging expert readers.

topics.name: Cohesion versus coherence
topics.description: Distinguish cohesion — the explicit lexical and grammatical ties between sentences (reference, conjunction, substitution, ellipsis, lexical relations) — from coherence, the reader's sense that a text has a consistent topic, purpose and logical development. The distinction lets learners see that linking devices cannot rescue a text whose ideas are not ordered or connected, and that coherent texts often leave some relations implicit.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the cohesive ties linking a pair of sentences and names their type (reference, conjunction, lexical)
Explains why a passage with many connectors can still be hard to follow, locating the missing logical or topical link
Distinguishes a cohesion problem (an ambiguous 'this') from a coherence problem (sentences that do not serve one point) in a sample text
Revises an incoherent paragraph by reordering or supplying a missing step of reasoning rather than by inserting connectors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two versions of a short paragraph: one dense with connectors but containing an unstated logical leap, and one with few connectors but clear topical and logical progression. Ask which is easier to follow and why. A secure learner prefers the second and locates the leap in the first; an insecure learner equates more connectors with better organisation.

topics.name: Lexical cohesion and reference chains
topics.description: Keep a topic in view across sentences through repetition, synonymy, hyponymy and superordinate or general nouns, combined with pronoun and article reference, so that the reader can track each participant through a text. Controlled reference chains are a major source of cohesion in academic prose, which repeats key nouns more than learners trained to 'avoid repetition' tend to expect.
masteryEvidence: Traces the reference chain for a key participant through an academic paragraph, listing each realisation (repetition, pronoun, synonym, superordinate)
Repeats a key noun where a pronoun would have two possible antecedents
Selects a superordinate or general noun (these organisms, such measures) to refer back to a set of previously named items
Shifts from indefinite or zero article to 'the' for second mention of a specific referent
Revises a passage in which a synonym substitution implies a new referent
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 120-word paragraph in which 'it' and 'they' could each refer to two antecedents and in which a synonym silently shifts the referent (participants → students → people). Ask the learner to mark each chain in a different colour and repair any ambiguity. Check whether both problems are found and fixed with repetition or a precise general noun rather than another pronoun.

topics.name: Linking adverbials and connectors
topics.description: Use additive, adversative, causal, sequential and summative linking adverbials (in addition, however, therefore, first, overall) to make relations between sentences explicit where the reader needs them, with expert-like frequency, placement and punctuation. Learner corpora show, varying by learner group, overuse of some connectors, underuse of others, a preference for sentence-initial position and mismatches between connector and relation, so the aim is selective rather than maximal use.
masteryEvidence: Classifies common linking adverbials by the relation they signal (addition, contrast/concession, result, sequence, summation, apposition)
Uses a linking adverbial only where the relation would otherwise be unclear, rather than at the start of most sentences
Places linking adverbials in initial and medial positions and punctuates them correctly between independent clauses
Distinguishes linking adverbials from coordinators and subordinators when combining clauses
Replaces speech-like connectors (Also, So, Besides) with register-appropriate choices in formal writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a 150-word paragraph explaining a cause and its consequences from a short set of notes. Count linking adverbials per sentence, check each one against the actual relation, and note any comma splices with 'however'. A secure learner uses two or three well-chosen connectors in varied positions; an insecure one opens nearly every sentence with a connector or mismatches connector and relation.

topics.name: Precise logical relations
topics.description: Choose between connectors with related but distinct meanings and grammar — however, whereas, although, in contrast, on the contrary, nevertheless; therefore, thus, hence, consequently — according to the exact relation (contrast, concession or correction; inference or consequence) and the clause structure each requires. Precision here distinguishes argument that is clear from text that merely sounds connected.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes contrast (whereas, in contrast), concession (although, nevertheless) and correction (on the contrary) and uses each appropriately
Constructs and punctuates subordinate clauses (although, whereas, while) and linking adverbials (however, nevertheless) correctly
Chooses among therefore, thus, hence and consequently according to whether the relation is inference or real-world consequence and according to register
Explains how replacing one connector with another in a sample sentence changes the claim made
Removes connectors that assert a relation the content does not support, such as 'therefore' after unrelated premises
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sentence pairs with the connector gapped, including one where 'on the contrary' and 'in contrast' compete and one where 'although' requires combining the pair into a single sentence. Ask for the best choice and a one-line justification. Check that the justification names the relation rather than 'it sounds right', and that subordinators are integrated grammatically.

topics.name: Given–new information structure
topics.description: Understand and apply the tendency in English for clauses to begin with information the reader already has (given) and to end with new or newsworthy information, using choices such as voice, a different grammatical subject or a summarising noun phrase to achieve this. Respecting given–new order is a main reason expert prose reads smoothly with relatively few connectors.
masteryEvidence: Identifies given and new information in each clause of a short academic paragraph, relative to the preceding sentence
Rewrites a clause so that information linked to the previous sentence comes first, using passive voice, a different subject or a summarising noun phrase
Explains why the choice between active and passive in a given sentence depends on the preceding context rather than on a rule about objectivity
Places long, heavy or newsworthy elements towards the end of the clause
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a three-sentence passage in which the second sentence begins with new information and ends with what was just mentioned. Ask the learner to improve the flow without changing meaning. A secure learner reorders the clause, often with a passive or a summarising noun subject, and justifies the change by pointing to the previous sentence.

topics.name: Thematic progression
topics.description: Manage the sequence of clause themes across a paragraph using Daneš's patterns — constant theme, linear progression in which the rheme of one clause becomes the next theme, and themes derived from a hypertheme — to move an argument forward while keeping it anchored. The patterns give writers a practical diagnostic for paragraphs that feel either repetitive or disjointed.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the theme of each sentence in a paragraph and labels the progression pattern
Diagnoses a disjointed paragraph as one whose themes do not pick up an earlier rheme or the hypertheme
Rewrites a paragraph to create linear progression, for example by nominalising the previous rheme as the next theme
Writes a topic sentence whose elements become the derived themes of later sentences
Varies patterns to avoid a monotonous run of identical themes in extended description
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to underline the theme (everything up to and including the subject) of each sentence in a recent paragraph of their own and to draw an arrow from each theme to the earlier element it picks up. Check whether they find any sentence whose theme links to nothing and can propose a revision that restores a link.

topics.name: Encapsulation with signalling nouns
topics.description: Use signalling (shell) nouns with a demonstrative or definite determiner — this approach, these findings, such a view, the problem is that — to encapsulate a preceding stretch of text or set up a following one, labelling it as a claim, problem, finding or limitation. Encapsulation links sentences while also categorising, and often evaluating, what has just been said.
masteryEvidence: Replaces a bare sentence-initial 'This' with 'this + noun' that accurately labels the preceding content
Chooses a signalling noun whose meaning matches the stretch it encapsulates (finding, claim, assumption, limitation)
Uses signalling nouns cataphorically to set up following content (The difficulty is that…; Two factors…)
Recognises the evaluative force of labels such as claim, assertion or misconception and uses them deliberately
Replaces vague labels (this thing, this issue) with a more precise noun where one is available
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph containing three sentence-initial instances of 'This' with no noun. Ask the learner to add a noun to each. Check the accuracy of each label (not 'this finding' for a hypothesis) and whether the learner can say what each label implies about the writer's stance.

topics.name: Text structure patterns
topics.description: Recognise and use recurrent text patterns — problem–solution (situation, problem, response, evaluation), general–specific, claim–counterclaim (hypothetical–real) and matching (comparison) — that organise stretches longer than a sentence and set up reader expectations. Knowing these patterns supports efficient reading, because readers can predict what comes next from lexical signals, and gives writers a frame for organising paragraphs and sections.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the pattern organising an academic passage and labels its elements (for example situation, problem, response, evaluation)
Locates lexical signals of each element (difficulty, approach, effective, however, in fact) in a text
Predicts the likely next element of an incomplete passage from its pattern and signals
Organises a paragraph or short section according to a pattern suited to the task, including a negative evaluation that restarts the cycle where appropriate
Recognises a claim–counterclaim structure in which a writer reports a view in order to reject or qualify it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 250-word passage with its final paragraph removed. Ask the learner to identify the pattern, name its elements so far and predict what the missing paragraph will do. Check that the prediction is supported by signals in the text (evaluative adjectives, 'however', problem vocabulary) rather than by topic knowledge alone.

topics.name: Frame markers and advance organisers
topics.description: Use frame markers — sequencing (first, finally), stage labels (to summarise, overall), goal announcements (this essay argues, the aim of this section is) and topic shifts (turning to, with regard to) — to make the organisation of an extended text visible at a density suited to its length and genre. Frame markers are an interactive metadiscourse resource that eases the reader's processing; they should not substitute for content.
masteryEvidence: Writes an introduction roadmap that previews the line of argument, not just a list of topics, in proportion to the text's length
Labels stages and marks topic shifts at section boundaries in extended writing
Distinguishes appropriate metatext in a dissertation chapter from excessive metatext in a short essay
Replaces procedural metatext (In this paragraph I will talk about…) with propositional signposting (This section shows that…)
Uses frame markers in published articles to navigate them selectively
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 2,000-word essay brief and ask the learner to write the final two sentences of the introduction. Then ask what would change for a 12,000-word dissertation chapter. Check that the roadmap signals the argument rather than listing topics and that the learner scales the amount of metatext to text length.

topics.name: Transitions between paragraphs and sections
topics.description: Link one paragraph or section to the next with bridging sentences or clauses that state how the coming point relates to the previous one — extends, contrasts with, qualifies or applies it — typically by encapsulating the prior point and announcing the new one. Effective transitions make the line of argument visible across units instead of leaving each paragraph as a free-standing block.
masteryEvidence: Writes paragraph openings that refer back to the previous point and state the new one (While cost explains part of the decline, it does not account for…)
Identifies the relation between consecutive paragraphs in a reverse outline (extension, contrast, consequence, application)
Bridges sections with encapsulating noun phrases rather than with bare connectors
Reorders a sequence of paragraphs whose current order obscures the argument
Distinguishes a relational transition from a merely additive opening (Another point is…)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner the last sentence of one paragraph and the topic of the next, and ask for an opening sentence. Then show a draft whose paragraphs all begin 'Another factor is…' and ask how the sequence could be made to argue. Check that the bridge names the relation and encapsulates the previous point.

topics.name: Terminological consistency
topics.description: Keep key technical and conceptual terms constant once introduced, varying wording only where the referent genuinely differs, so that readers do not infer distinctions the writer does not intend. In academic writing a change of term is often read as a change of concept, so the 'elegant variation' rewarded in some other kinds of writing can mislead.
masteryEvidence: Lists the key terms of their own text and checks that each is used with one meaning and one form throughout
Defines or glosses a key term on first use and uses that term thereafter
Distinguishes near-synonyms that are interchangeable in context from those that name distinct constructs in their field
Signals explicitly when a different term is introduced for a related but distinct concept
Keeps abbreviations, variable names and labels consistent across text, tables and figures
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to take a 600-word section of their own draft and list every expression used for its two central concepts. Check whether the variants refer to the same thing and whether any variation would lead a reader in the field to assume a different construct; ask the learner to justify any variation they keep.

topics.name: Making reasoning explicit for the reader
topics.description: Understand the expectation, common in English-medium academic writing, that the writer rather than the reader is responsible for making purpose, structure and logical connections explicit, and recognise this as a convention that varies across disciplines, genres and writing traditions rather than a universal standard of good writing. The concept helps learners interpret feedback such as 'unclear' or 'make the link explicit' and decide how much to spell out for a given reader.
masteryEvidence: Explains the reader/writer responsibility distinction and what it implies for explicit thesis statements, topic sentences and links
Identifies points in their own draft where a reader would have to infer an unstated connection, and states it
Adjusts explicitness for different readers (expert examiner, non-specialist, peer)
Discusses the concept critically, recognising variation within English and the risk of stereotyping other writing traditions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph whose main claim appears only implicitly in its last sentence and whose evidence-to-claim links are unstated. Ask how a marker in the learner's target programme might respond and what the learner would change, then ask whether the original could work well in another context. A strong answer revises for explicitness while recognising that the original is not illogical.

topics.name: Signposting in spoken academic discourse
topics.description: Use and recognise macro-markers (Let's move on to…, What I want to focus on today is…) and micro-markers (so, now, right) together with pausing and intonation to organise spoken academic discourse in lectures, presentations and seminars. Because listeners cannot scan back, explicit structural signalling carries more of the organisational load in speech than in writing.
masteryEvidence: Identifies macro-markers in a recorded lecture and uses them to reconstruct its structure in notes
Distinguishes structuring markers from markers that flag importance or relevance
Uses macro-markers to preview, move between and summarise the sections of a short presentation
Combines verbal markers with a pause or change of pitch at section boundaries
Uses spoken rather than written-style connectors (So, Now, The next thing is rather than Furthermore, Moreover) when speaking
topics.assessmentPrompt: Play a three- to four-minute lecture extract and ask the learner to note each point where the speaker changes topic and the words that signalled it. Then ask for a one-minute spoken explanation of a process using at least two macro-markers. Check accurate identification of boundaries and natural spoken markers in production.

topics.name: Defining terms
topics.description: Define terms using formal sentence definitions (term + class + distinguishing features), extended definitions that add examples, contrasts or history, operational definitions that state how a concept is measured or identified, and discussion of contested definitions that compares how different authors define a term. Defining establishes shared ground and shows readers how the writer is using key concepts.
masteryEvidence: Writes a formal definition with an appropriate superordinate class and distinguishing features, using a defining relative clause
Extends a definition with an example, a contrast with a related term or relevant background, as the task requires
Writes an operational definition stating how a concept is measured or identified in a study
Compares competing definitions of a contested term from sources and states which the writer adopts and why
Avoids circular definitions and general-dictionary definitions where a disciplinary definition is needed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to define a key term from their field in one sentence, then to extend it into a short paragraph for a reader new to the field. Check for a suitable class word and distinguishing features, absence of circularity, and whether the extension adds genuine information (an example, a contrast or a source-based definition).

topics.name: Classifying and categorising
topics.description: Classify phenomena by stating the basis of classification, the categories and their members, using language such as can be divided into, falls into, comprises, is classified according to and consists of. Clear classification rests on a consistent criterion and categories that are mutually exclusive and, where intended, exhaustive.
masteryEvidence: States the criterion (basis) of a classification explicitly
Produces categories consistent with a single criterion and identifies overlapping or missing categories in a given scheme
Uses classification verbs and their grammar accurately (consist of, comprise, be divided into, fall into)
Describes a classification shown in a tree diagram or table in continuous prose
Discusses the limits of a classification scheme, such as borderline cases or alternative criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a tree diagram (for example types of research data or of renewable energy) and ask for a short paragraph describing it. Then ask what criterion underlies the scheme and whether any item could belong to two categories. Check verb grammar, explicit statement of the basis and awareness of overlap.

topics.name: Describing processes and procedures
topics.description: Describe natural, experimental and technical processes and procedures in a clear sequence, using sequencing devices, passive voice where the agent is unimportant, purpose expressions (to + infinitive, in order to, so that) and time clauses. Process description underpins methods sections, laboratory and technical reports, and explanations of how phenomena occur.
masteryEvidence: Describes a process in logical order with varied sequencing devices and time clauses rather than repeated 'then'
Chooses passive or active voice according to whether the agent matters
Expresses the purpose of steps with to-infinitive, in order to and so that
Distinguishes a general process (present simple) from a completed procedure in a study (past simple)
Converts a flowchart or process diagram into continuous prose
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a five-stage flowchart (for example water treatment or a laboratory procedure) and ask for a paragraph describing it as a general process, then two sentences describing it as a procedure carried out in a study. Check the tense shift, the voice choices, purpose expressions and variety of sequencing.

topics.name: Describing structures and systems
topics.description: Describe the structure of physical objects, organisations and systems in terms of parts and wholes (consists of, comprises, is made up of), spatial relations (adjacent to, at the base of, connected to) and the functions of components (serves to, is responsible for). Structural description is essential in science, engineering, design, anatomy, geography and organisational studies.
masteryEvidence: Describes an object or system from whole to parts in a logical spatial or hierarchical order
Uses part–whole verbs (consist of, comprise, contain, include) with correct complementation
Uses spatial prepositions and expressions precisely
Links components to their functions using function language (serves to, enables, is used for)
Describes an organisational chart or labelled diagram so that a reader could reconstruct it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a labelled diagram (for example a cell, a circuit or an organisational structure) and ask the learner to describe it for a reader who cannot see it; a partner then draws from the description. Check part–whole verbs, spatial precision, function language and logical order by comparing the drawing with the original.

topics.name: Comparing and contrasting
topics.description: Compare and contrast entities, theories, methods or data against explicit criteria using similarity and difference language (similarly, likewise, whereas, in contrast, differ in, share, unlike) and comparative structures, and organise extended comparisons point by point or in blocks according to purpose. Academic comparison is led by criteria and arrives at a point, rather than listing similarities and differences.
masteryEvidence: Identifies or chooses explicit criteria for comparison suited to the task
Uses similarity and difference language and comparative structures accurately, including degree (considerably, slightly)
Organises a comparison point by point or in blocks and explains why that organisation suits the purpose
Draws a conclusion or judgement from a comparison rather than ending with a list
Avoids incomplete or illogical comparisons (comparing one country's GDP with another country)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a table comparing two approaches on four criteria and ask for a 150-word comparison that leads to a recommendation. Check criterion-led organisation, accurate comparative structures (including 'than that of'), and a concluding point that follows from the comparison.

topics.name: Expressing cause and effect
topics.description: Express causal relations through conjunctions (because, since, so), prepositions (due to, owing to, as a result of), verbs (lead to, result in, contribute to, stem from), nouns (a cause of, a consequence of, a factor in) and adjectives (attributable to, responsible for), and calibrate the strength of the causal claim (causes, is associated with, may contribute to). Much academic explanation packs causation into verbs and noun phrases rather than linking clauses with conjunctions.
masteryEvidence: Expresses the same causal relation through conjunction, preposition, verb and noun structures
Uses causal verbs with correct direction and complementation (result in versus result from; lead to + noun or -ing)
Uses associational rather than causal language where the evidence shows only a correlation
Distinguishes single, multiple and chained causes and expresses each clearly
Uses nominalised causal structures to link sentences (This increase led to…)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short description of a correlational finding and a short summary of an experiment. Ask for one sentence summarising the causal implication of each. Check whether the learner uses causal verbs for the experiment and associational language for the correlation, and whether 'result in/from' and 'due to' are used correctly.

topics.name: Exemplifying and illustrating
topics.description: Illustrate general statements with examples and cases using exemplification language (for example, for instance, such as, a case in point is, as illustrated by) and choose examples that are representative and relevant, linking them explicitly back to the point they support. Examples make abstract claims concrete, but they carry argumentative weight only when their relevance is made clear.
masteryEvidence: Uses for example and for instance (sentence level) and such as and e.g. (phrase level) with correct grammar and punctuation
Chooses examples that are representative of the general claim rather than exceptional
Links an example explicitly back to the claim it illustrates (This illustrates…)
Distinguishes an example that illustrates a claim from evidence that establishes it
Develops an extended example or case within a paragraph without losing the controlling idea
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a general claim from the learner's field and ask for one brief and one extended example in support. Check grammatical control (such as + noun phrase, not a clause), the representativeness of the examples, and whether the extended example is linked back to the claim.

topics.name: Problem, solution and evaluation
topics.description: Present situations, problems, responses and evaluations using problem vocabulary (challenge, constraint, drawback), response vocabulary (approach, measure, intervention) and evaluative language that judges whether responses work, including cycles in which a response creates a new problem. This function organises problem–solution essays, case studies, reports and the gap-identifying moves of research introductions.
masteryEvidence: Organises a text or section around situation, problem, response and evaluation, with each element recognisable
Uses problem, response and evaluation vocabulary precisely and with conventional collocation (address a problem, mitigate a risk)
Evaluates proposed responses against criteria such as effectiveness, cost and feasibility rather than only describing them
Writes recursive sequences in which a negatively evaluated response leads to a further response
Distinguishes the causes of a problem from its consequences or symptoms
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a brief case scenario and ask for a 200-word problem–solution paragraph. Check that each element is present and signalled, that at least one response is evaluated against a stated criterion, and that causes of the problem are not confused with its symptoms.

topics.name: Explaining and justifying
topics.description: Explain how and why phenomena occur and justify decisions or claims by giving reasons, mechanisms and rationales, using language such as because, since, which explains why, this is because, the reason for and the rationale for. Explanation goes beyond stating that something happens to show the mechanism or reasoning behind it, which is much of what markers mean by 'analysis'.
masteryEvidence: Explains a mechanism as a sequence of causal steps rather than a single 'because'
Justifies a choice (of method, source or option) with a reason linked to purpose or criteria
Uses sentential relatives and explanatory noun structures correctly (which explains why; the reason for X is that), avoiding 'the reason is because' in formal writing
Offers and weighs alternative explanations for an observation or result
Distinguishes explanation from description in their own writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show a simple graph with an unexpected result and ask the learner to account for it in a paragraph. Check whether they move from description to mechanism, offer more than one possible explanation, weigh them, and use explanatory structures correctly.

topics.name: Predicting and hypothesising
topics.description: Predict outcomes and formulate hypotheses using predictive and speculative language — modal verbs (will, would, may, is likely to), conditionals, hypothesis frames (it is hypothesised that, would be expected to) and conditions on predictions (provided that, assuming that) — distinguishing confident predictions from tentative speculation. Hypothesising is central to research proposals, experimental reports, discussions of implications and thought experiments.
masteryEvidence: Formulates a testable hypothesis or prediction in one clear sentence with explicit variables or conditions
Uses will, would, is likely to and may to mark degrees of predictive confidence
Uses real and unreal conditionals to reason about predicted outcomes and counterfactuals
Distinguishes a hypothesis (to be tested) from a finding (already established) through tense and modality
Speculates about implications or future developments with appropriate hedging
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a research question and ask for a hypothesis, a statement of what result would support it, and one sentence on what an unexpected result would imply. Check modal and conditional accuracy and whether the hypothesis is testable rather than a restatement of the question.

topics.name: Recommending
topics.description: Make recommendations that follow from analysis, using modal and lexical resources (should, it is recommended that, it is advisable to), the mandative subjunctive or should-alternative (It is essential that each participant be informed), and language of priority, feasibility and conditions (in the first instance, where resources allow). Effective recommendations are specific, justified by the preceding analysis and pitched to the reader's authority to act.
masteryEvidence: Writes recommendations that are explicitly linked to findings or analysis
Uses should, it is recommended that and the mandative subjunctive (or should + infinitive) accurately
Specifies who should act, what action is recommended and under what conditions or timescale
Prioritises and qualifies recommendations by feasibility, cost or strength of evidence
Adjusts the directness of recommendations to genre and readership (a client report versus implications in a research article)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short summary of findings from a case and ask for three recommendations. Check the link to findings, specificity (actor, action, condition), accurate mandative structures, and whether the most strongly worded recommendation rests on the strongest evidence.

topics.name: Summarising and concluding
topics.description: Summarise one's own preceding content and draw conclusions from it, using summative and inferential language (Overall, In sum, Taken together, These findings suggest, It can therefore be concluded that), so that a section or text ends by stating what has been established and what follows. This function differs from summarising a source: it consolidates the writer's own argument or results.
masteryEvidence: Writes a concluding sentence or paragraph that synthesises preceding points rather than repeating them in order
Draws an inference from the synthesised points with appropriately calibrated language
Uses summative markers in proportion to text length rather than after every paragraph
Includes implications and limitations in a conclusion without introducing new evidence
Encapsulates preceding results with 'these + noun' before drawing a conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short paragraphs presenting related findings and ask for a two-sentence conclusion. Check that it synthesises (says what the findings have in common or add up to) rather than lists, and that the inference is hedged in line with the evidence.

topics.name: Chronological narration
topics.description: Narrate events and developments in chronological order using time expressions (in the early 1990s, over the following decade, by 2010), periodisation (the post-war period, the first phase), tense and aspect sequences (past simple, past perfect, present perfect for developments continuing to now) and time clauses. This function is needed in historical accounts, case histories, methodology recounts and literature reviews that trace the development of a field.
masteryEvidence: Sequences events with varied time expressions and time clauses
Uses past perfect for prior events and present perfect for developments continuing to the present, appropriately
Groups a sequence into labelled phases and explains the basis of the periodisation
Moves from recounting events to interpreting their significance
Writes a case history or methodology recount that a reader can follow in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a timeline of six events in the development of a field and ask for a paragraph tracing it, ending with a comment on its significance. Check tense choices, variety of time expressions, grouping into phases and an interpretive final sentence.

topics.name: Evaluating strengths, weaknesses and significance
topics.description: Evaluate ideas, evidence, methods, solutions or texts by stating explicit criteria, weighing strengths against weaknesses and reaching a judgement of value or significance, using evaluative lexis (robust, limited, compelling, a shortcoming), comparative evaluation and balanced structures (While X…, Y). Evaluation is a large part of what distinguishes critical from descriptive academic writing.
masteryEvidence: States the criteria by which something is evaluated (validity, cost, relevance, generalisability)
Identifies strengths and weaknesses and weighs them to reach an overall judgement
Uses evaluative adjectives, nouns and adverbs precisely and with appropriate strength
States the significance of a finding or argument for the field or the task question
Distinguishes evaluation from description and from unsupported personal opinion in their own writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short description of a policy or study and ask for a 120-word evaluation. Check for explicit criteria, at least one strength and one weakness, an overall judgement that weighs them, and precise evaluative lexis rather than 'good', 'bad' or 'interesting'.

topics.name: Metadiscourse
topics.description: Understand metadiscourse as the resources by which writers and speakers organise a text for its reader (interactive: transitions, frame markers, endophoric markers, evidentials, code glosses) and express attitudes and engage the reader (interactional: hedges, boosters, attitude markers, self-mention, engagement markers). The concept gives learners a unified way of seeing academic writing as interaction with a reader rather than as neutral presentation of content.
masteryEvidence: Classifies metadiscourse items in an academic text as interactive or interactional and names their subcategory
Explains the function of a metadiscourse item in its context rather than by its form alone
Compares metadiscourse in two disciplines or genres and suggests reasons for the differences
Identifies under- or over-use of a metadiscourse category in their own draft and revises accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 200-word discussion paragraph from a published article. Ask the learner to highlight three interactive and three interactional items and explain what each does for the reader. Check that classification is functional (for example 'in other words' as a code gloss) and that the learner notices items whose function depends on context, such as 'clearly' as a booster versus a manner adverb.

topics.name: Hedging devices
topics.description: Use hedging devices — modal verbs (may, might, could), lexical verbs (suggest, appear, indicate), adverbs and adjectives (possibly, likely), approximators (approximately, to some extent) and impersonal frames (it seems that, it is possible that) — to present claims with appropriate tentativeness, mark the writer's precision about evidence and show deference to readers and the field. Hedging is central to how academic claims are negotiated and accepted.
masteryEvidence: Identifies hedges in an academic text and distinguishes those qualifying the accuracy of a claim from those softening the writer's commitment towards readers
Uses a range of hedging devices beyond 'may', including lexical verbs, adverbs, approximators and impersonal frames
Places the hedge on the part of the claim that is uncertain (cause, scope or degree)
Avoids stacking several hedges on one claim where one suffices
Varies hedging density across a text, hedging interpretations more than descriptions of method
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three unhedged claims based on a short results summary (for example a correlation found in one small sample). Ask the learner to rewrite each so that it is defensible. Check the variety of devices, whether each hedge targets the actual source of uncertainty, and whether any claim has become so hedged that it says nothing.

topics.name: Boosters
topics.description: Use boosters — adverbs (clearly, undoubtedly), verbs (show, demonstrate, establish), and impersonal frames (it is evident that, there is no doubt that) — to express justified certainty and solidarity with readers, and recognise when certainty is unwarranted or rhetorically risky. Together with hedges, boosters let writers mark which claims they are prepared to stand behind.
masteryEvidence: Identifies boosters in academic texts and explains what degree of certainty each claims
Chooses reporting and research verbs by commitment (suggest, indicate, show, demonstrate, prove) according to the evidence
Uses boosters selectively for well-established findings or the writer's central claim
Replaces speech-like intensifiers (very, really, totally, extremely) with precise statements of degree
Recognises that 'obviously' and 'of course' presuppose shared knowledge that some readers may not have
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a student paragraph containing several boosters (clearly, proves, obviously, definitely). Ask the learner which are justified by the evidence given and to revise the rest. Check that 'proves' is downgraded for empirical findings and that at least one justified booster is retained rather than every one being hedged.

topics.name: Calibrating claims to evidence
topics.description: Match the strength of each claim to the type, quality and quantity of evidence and to the scope of the data, choosing among assertion, boosting, hedging and limitation of scope so that claims are neither overstated nor hedged into vacuity. Calibration is a reasoning skill realised in language: the writer first judges what the evidence licenses and then chooses wording.
masteryEvidence: Judges what claim a body of evidence supports (correlational or experimental; one study or many) before writing it
Adjusts claim strength along the dimensions of scope (all, most, some), certainty (shows, suggests) and generality (in this sample, in general)
Distinguishes the strength of a finding from the strength of the writer's interpretation of it
Revises both over-claimed and over-hedged sentences in their own and others' writing
Explains to a peer why a claim is miscalibrated, with reference to the evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present a brief study summary (design, sample, result) and four candidate claims ranging from 'proves' to 'may possibly suggest in some cases'. Ask the learner to choose the best-calibrated claim and justify it with reference to design and sample. Check that the reasoning addresses the evidence, not only word choice.

topics.name: Attitude markers
topics.description: Use attitude markers — evaluative adverbs (surprisingly, importantly, unfortunately), adjectives (striking, notable, problematic) and frames (it is notable that, a key limitation is) — to signal the writer's affective and evaluative stance towards propositions, and judge when explicit evaluation strengthens or weakens an academic text. Such markers direct readers to what the writer considers significant, surprising or problematic.
masteryEvidence: Identifies attitude markers and the evaluation each expresses (importance, surprise, concern, agreement)
Uses attitude markers to foreground the significance of key findings or arguments
Distinguishes evaluation appropriate to academic texts from emotive personal reaction (I was shocked that)
Selects evaluative adjectives with precise meaning and conventional collocation (a robust finding, a serious limitation)
Recognises differences between disciplines in how densely attitude is marked
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a results paragraph containing no evaluation and ask the learner to add two attitude markers that would guide a reader to the most important finding. Check that the evaluation is anchored in the data, uses academic rather than emotive lexis, and is placed where it matters.

topics.name: Self-mention and authorial roles
topics.description: Use first-person pronouns and alternatives (I, we, the present study, this thesis) to construct authorial roles — from representative of a wider group (generic 'we') and guide through the text, through architect of its structure and recounter of procedures, to opinion-holder and originator of ideas — in line with disciplinary and genre norms. Self-mention is a choice about presence and responsibility, not a matter of a blanket rule for or against 'I'.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the role a first-person pronoun plays in a sentence (representative, guide, architect, recounter, opinion-holder, originator)
Uses self-mention where it is conventional in their discipline and genre, and impersonal alternatives where those are
Uses 'I' or 'we' to take responsibility for interpretations and contributions, not only for procedures
Avoids author-'we' for a single author unless it is a field convention, and avoids inclusive 'we' that overgeneralises
Explains, with evidence from their field, why 'never use I' is not a universal rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three sentences from different disciplines that use 'I' or 'we' and ask the learner to identify the role each plays and whether a student in their own field could write it. Then ask them to rewrite one impersonal claim from their draft with self-mention and explain how responsibility for the claim changes.

topics.name: Reader engagement
topics.description: Use reader-engagement resources — inclusive 'we' and other reader references, directives (note that, consider, see Table 2), questions, appeals to shared knowledge (as is well known) and personal asides — to bring readers into the argument, guide their interpretation and build solidarity, at a level suited to discipline and genre.
masteryEvidence: Identifies engagement markers in academic texts and the reader role each assumes
Uses directives to guide readers to textual or cognitive actions (see Table 2; note that; consider the case of)
Uses a question to frame a problem or research focus rather than as a substitute for a claim
Uses inclusive 'we' and appeals to shared knowledge only where the shared ground genuinely exists for the intended readers
Adjusts the density and type of engagement across genres (textbook, research article, essay, lay summary)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give an introductory paragraph from a textbook and one from a research article on a similar topic. Ask the learner to find the engagement markers and explain the difference in density and type, then rewrite one sentence of their own to include a directive or question. Check that the choice suits the genre and does not presume knowledge the reader may lack.

topics.name: Generalising and qualifying
topics.description: Make generalisations whose scope matches the evidence by using quantifiers and frequency expressions (most, many, a minority of, often, rarely), tendency expressions (tend to, are inclined to), approximators (broadly, largely, in general) and scope limiters (in most cases, with some exceptions, in this context). Bounded generalisation avoids both sweeping claims and lists of particulars that never reach a general point.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites sweeping generalisations (everyone, always, all societies) as bounded claims appropriate to the evidence

Uses tend to, frequency adverbs and quantifiers accurately, including their grammar (tend + to-infinitive; most + plural noun without 'of' but most of + determiner + noun: most students, most of the students)
States the population, context or conditions to which a generalisation applies
Distinguishes a claim about a category from a claim about every member of it
Moves from a set of examples to a stated general pattern
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five sweeping statements typical of essay openings (for example 'Nowadays everyone uses social media'). Ask the learner to rewrite each as a defensible claim. Check the range of devices, grammatical accuracy and whether the rewrites specify scope rather than only adding 'may'.

topics.name: Averral versus attribution
topics.description: Distinguish propositions the writer avers (takes responsibility for) from those attributed to other sources, and track this distinction in reading and writing so that it is always clear whose claim is whose and how far the writer endorses it. Because unsignalled statements are read as the writer's own averral, failing to mark attribution or its boundary affects both the argument and academic integrity.
masteryEvidence: Identifies, clause by clause, whether a proposition in an academic text is averred or attributed, citing the linguistic signal
Explains that statements without attribution signals are read as the writer's own claims
Marks where attributed content ends and the writer's own comment begins in source-based writing
Explains how a writer can attribute a view without endorsing it (X claims that…) or while endorsing it (as X shows…)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 150-word literature-review paragraph drawing on three sources with some writer comment. Ask the learner to colour-code each clause as averred or attributed and name the signal. Check how they treat sentences that follow a citation and continue the source's content without a new signal: a secure learner flags these as ambiguous.

topics.name: Language of concession and counter-argument
topics.description: Use the language of concession and counter-argument — subordinators (although, while, even though), adverbials (admittedly, nevertheless, nonetheless), impersonal frames (it could be argued that, it is true that…, but) and limiting moves (this does not mean that) — to acknowledge an opposing point and then limit or outweigh it. When followed by an effective counter, concession signals fairness and anticipates objections, strengthening rather than weakening an argument.
masteryEvidence: Constructs concession–counter sequences within a sentence (Although X, Y) and across sentences (Admittedly, X. However, Y.)
Distinguishes concession from simple contrast and uses each appropriately
Raises a counter-argument with an impersonal frame without appearing to endorse it (It might be objected that…)
Follows each concession with a counter that states how far the conceded point limits the writer's claim
Structures and punctuates concessive clauses correctly, without double marking (although…but)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a thesis statement and one strong objection to it. Ask the learner to write two or three sentences acknowledging and responding to the objection. Check grammatical control of the concessive structure, that the concession is fairly stated rather than a straw man, and that the response limits the objection rather than merely contradicting it.

topics.name: Opening and closing space for other voices
topics.description: Position a text in relation to other voices by expanding the dialogue (entertaining possibilities, attributing views to others) or contracting it (denying, countering, concurring, pronouncing, endorsing), as described in the engagement system of appraisal theory. Control of these options lets writers acknowledge alternatives while steering readers towards their own position, a pattern associated with highly rated academic argument.
masteryEvidence: Classifies stance options in a text as expanding (entertain, attribute) or contracting (deny, counter, concur, pronounce, endorse)
Analyses how a published introduction or discussion opens and then closes dialogic space across a paragraph

Chooses between endorsing attribution (X shows, X demonstrates), which contracts the dialogue, and acknowledging (X reports, X argues) or distancing (X claims) attribution, which keeps it open, according to the writer's position
Revises a paragraph of bare assertions to acknowledge relevant alternative positions before contracting towards the writer's claim
Explains how the sequence of expanding and contracting moves leads the reader to a conclusion
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph from a highly rated student discussion section and ask the learner to label each clause as expanding, contracting or bare assertion, then explain how the writer leads the reader to the final claim. Follow up with a request for a two-sentence move on a debate in the learner's field that first opens and then narrows the dialogue. Check accurate labelling and a counter that limits rather than ignores the alternative.

topics.name: Language for evaluating others' work
topics.description: Use language that evaluates other scholars' work fairly and precisely — evaluative reporting verbs and adjectives, praise–criticism pairs and mitigated critique (While X offers…, it overlooks…; a limitation of this study is…) — so that critique is specific, justified and collegial. This language is central to literature reviews, critiques, peer review and positioning one's own research.
masteryEvidence: Uses evaluative reporting verbs and adjectives that convey the intended judgement (convincingly demonstrates; asserts without evidence)
Constructs praise–criticism pairs that acknowledge a strength before stating a limitation
Directs critique at specific aspects of a work (sample, measures, theoretical framing) rather than at the work or author as a whole
Adjusts the directness of criticism to genre and audience (literature review, critique assignment, peer review report)
Distinguishes reporting a limitation the authors acknowledge from raising one of their own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a short abstract and methods summary of a study with one clear limitation. Ask for two sentences evaluating it for a literature review. Check that the critique is specific, pairs acknowledgement with limitation, and uses evaluative verbs or adjectives deliberately rather than 'This study is good/bad'.

topics.name: Authorial voice
topics.description: Understand authorial voice as the identity and position a writer constructs through linguistic choices — stance markers, self-mention, the framing of sources and control of the argument's structure — and develop a voice that is distinct from, and in control of, the voices of sources. Voice is a textual achievement that can be analysed and taught, not an innate personal quality or simply the use of 'I'.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the linguistic features through which a writer's voice is constructed in a text (evaluation, self-mention, framing of sources, claim strength)
Keeps their own position visible across a source-based text, particularly in paragraph openings and closings
Uses sources to support their argument rather than letting the sequence of sources determine the text's structure
Explains how their voice differs across genres such as reflective writing, essays and research articles
Reflects on how adopting an academic voice relates to their wider identity as a multilingual writer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to take a source-heavy paragraph from their own draft and mark where their own position is stated or implied. If it is not visible in the first and last sentences, ask for a revision. Check whether the revised paragraph is led by a claim that the sources then support.

topics.name: Code glosses and exemplification
topics.description: Use code glosses to reformulate (that is, in other words, namely, i.e.) and to exemplify (for example, such as, e.g.) so that readers recover the intended meaning of a term, claim or category, judging what the intended reader needs explained. Code glosses are an interactive metadiscourse resource that reflects the writer's model of the reader's knowledge.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes reformulation markers (that is, in other words, namely) from exemplification markers (for example, such as)
Uses 'namely' and 'i.e.' to specify, and 'e.g.' and 'such as' to give non-exhaustive examples, with correct punctuation
Glosses technical terms or abstract claims where the intended reader would need it, and not otherwise
Uses parentheses and appositive noun phrases as compact glossing devices
Avoids reformulations that alter rather than clarify the original claim
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three sentences each containing an abstract term or claim and ask the learner to add one reformulating gloss and one exemplifying gloss. Check the i.e./e.g. distinction, punctuation, and whether each gloss genuinely clarifies for a non-specialist reader without changing the claim.

topics.name: Expressing stance in speech
topics.description: Express and recognise stance in spoken academic interaction — opinion frames (I'd argue, it seems to me), mitigated disagreement (I'm not entirely convinced that), vague language and approximation (sort of, more or less) and boosting (I'm fairly sure) — together with prosodic cues, so that speakers can take positions in seminars, presentations and supervisions while maintaining collegial relations.
masteryEvidence: Uses a range of spoken stance frames to state a position with appropriate tentativeness or conviction
Mitigates disagreement and criticism in discussion without abandoning the point being made
Recognises stance signalled by lecturers and peers through word choice and intonation, including scepticism
Uses vague language and approximation appropriately in speech while avoiding it where precision is required
Adjusts spoken stance to the setting (seminar, supervision, conference question session)
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a short seminar-style discussion of a contested reading, note the learner's stance expressions when agreeing, disagreeing and stating a view. Check range beyond 'I think', mitigation of disagreement, and whether the learner's position remains clear to other participants.

dependencies.reason: Knowing that cohesive ties serve the reader's tracking of topics frames lexical chains as a coherence tool rather than a vocabulary exercise
Reference chains interleave pronoun and demonstrative reference with lexical repetition, so unambiguous pronoun use is part of building a chain
Second mention of a specific referent is signalled by the shift to 'the', which is how many lexical chains are marked
Understanding that connectors signal but do not create logical relations is the basis for selective rather than maximal connector use
Using linking adverbials correctly depends on recognising independent clauses and how they are combined, as distinct from coordination and subordination
Fine distinctions among contrastive and resultative connectors presuppose control of the basic semantic categories of linking adverbials
Choosing between although/whereas and however/nevertheless requires control of subordinate clause structure as well as meaning
The passive is one of the main resources for moving given information into subject position, so control of its form makes the information-structure choice available
Thematic progression patterns describe how successive clause starting points pick up given information, so the given–new principle must be understood first
Linking a new theme to an earlier rheme is usually realised through repetition, synonymy or a general noun
Linear progression in academic prose typically nominalises the process in one rheme so that it can become the next theme
Encapsulation depends on a repertoire of abstract nouns (approach, factor, issue, finding) whose meaning is filled in by the co-text
The core structure is a demonstrative determiner plus noun, so control of this/these reference and its antecedents is required
Text patterns are a model of coherence above the sentence, so learners must first separate underlying organisation from surface linking
Sequencing and summative frame markers extend the linking adverbials learners already use between sentences to the level of the whole text
A transition relates one paragraph's controlling idea to the next, so writers need to be able to state each paragraph's point
Bridging sentences typically encapsulate the previous paragraph's point with a signalling noun phrase before introducing the new point
Effective transitions open with information carried over from the previous paragraph and end with the new point, applying given–new order at paragraph level
Consistency decisions require understanding how repetition and synonymy create or break reference chains
Learners need to recognise which words in their field function as defined technical terms that should not be varied
Judging whether two expressions can be used interchangeably depends on knowing how near-synonyms differ in meaning and strength
Writer responsibility concerns who makes coherence relations explicit, so the notion of coherence relations must already be in place
Deciding how much to make explicit depends on a model of the intended reader and the purpose of the text
Micro-markers and many macro-markers express the same additive, contrastive and sequential relations as written linking adverbials
Understanding that speech is processed in real time without the visual layout of writing explains why spoken discourse needs denser, differently worded signposting
Frame markers are a principal means by which writers take responsibility for making a text's organisation explicit to the reader
The formal definition frame (an X is a Y which/that…) depends on control of defining relative clauses
Formal definitions already place a term in a class; classification extends this to dividing a class by a criterion
Many classification structures are passive (can be divided into, are classified as), so passive form is needed
Describing processes where the agent is unknown or unimportant relies heavily on the passive
Sequential linking adverbials (first, subsequently, finally) organise the steps of a process
Spatial and part–whole description cannot be carried out without control of spatial and complex prepositions
Comparison relies on comparative and superlative structures, including degree and 'than that of' constructions
Contrastive and similarity linking adverbials (in contrast, similarly) connect points in an extended comparison
Within-sentence contrast with whereas and while requires control of subordinate clauses
Clausal expression of cause and result (because, since, so that) is the base on which other causal structures are built
Causal verbs and nouns have fixed complementation and direction (result in/from, contribute to, a factor in)
For example and for instance are linking adverbials whose position and punctuation follow the same rules
Such as introduces a postmodifying phrase within a noun phrase, so learners need to recognise noun-phrase structure to use it correctly
Part–whole and spatial description often uses passive and participial forms (is composed of, is connected to, is located at)
The problem–solution function realises one of the text patterns, so learners need the pattern's elements and signals before producing it
The evaluation element requires judging responses against criteria
Explaining mechanisms and reasons is built from causal relations expressed in a range of grammatical forms
Sentential relative clauses (…, which explains why…) are a common explanatory resource
Predictions and hypotheses are frequently framed as real or unreal conditionals
Most hypotheses predict a causal or associational relation between variables
Recommendation frames (it is recommended that, it is essential that) take that-clauses, including mandative forms
Recommendations typically follow the analysis of a problem and the evaluation of possible responses
Recommendations are qualified according to evidence and feasibility, which uses hedging resources
Summative linking adverbials (overall, in sum, to conclude) mark the move to concluding
Conclusions encapsulate preceding content with demonstrative reference (These results, This pattern)
Inferences drawn in conclusions are typically hedged in line with the evidence (This suggests…)
Narrating sequences and developments relies on contrasts between past simple, past perfect and present perfect
Criterion-based judgement often weighs alternatives against each other, drawing on comparison language
Producing evaluation deliberately requires the conceptual distinction between describing, analysing and evaluating
Sequential and temporal linking adverbials (subsequently, meanwhile, by then) organise narrated events across sentences
Frame markers are usually the first metadiscourse learners meet; the concept is best built by generalising from such familiar resources
Hedging gives learners a concrete interactional resource that the metadiscourse concept then situates alongside interactive ones
Modal verbs of likelihood are the most frequent hedging resource, and their epistemic meanings must be controlled before range is extended
Lexical hedges such as suggest, indicate and appear depend on knowing these verbs' meanings, strength and complementation
Calibration requires a repertoire of hedging devices with which to weaken claims to the level the evidence supports
Calibration also requires resources for committing firmly where evidence is strong, so that well-supported claims are not under-stated
Judging what a claim can be based on depends on knowing the relative strength of different kinds of evidence
Attitude markers are realised by evaluative adjectives, adverbs and nouns, so the lexical repertoire must be in place
The metadiscourse concept frames attitude marking as a reader-directed choice rather than a personal emotional reaction
Treating self-mention as one interactional resource among others helps learners see it as a rhetorical choice rather than a rule
Learners need to see personal pronouns as a formality tendency rather than a prohibition before they can make discipline-sensitive choices
Using reader-inclusive 'we' presupposes distinguishing it from the author-exclusive 'we' of self-mention
Appeals to shared knowledge (obviously, of course) overlap formally with boosters and carry the same risk of unwarranted certainty
Bounding a generalisation relies on accurate quantifiers (most, a minority of, few) and their grammar
Qualifying scope is one form of hedging; learners who already hedge certainty can extend this to quantity, frequency and context
Verbal boosters (show, demonstrate, establish) depend on knowing these verbs' meanings and relative strength
Replacing speech-like intensifiers with justified boosters depends on recognising intensifiers as a feature of informal register
Understanding that citation credits others and makes claims verifiable motivates tracking which claims belong to whom
Attribution is typically realised through a reporting clause with a that-complement, so learners must recognise where the attributed proposition begins and ends
Concession depends on distinguishing concessive connectors (although, nevertheless) from contrastive ones and controlling their grammar
Impersonal concessive frames (it could be argued that) use hedging resources to entertain a view without endorsing it
Expanding through attribution and contracting through endorsement or distancing both presuppose a clear grasp of averral versus attribution
The counter option in engagement is realised largely through concessive and adversative language
Entertaining and pronouncing are realised through hedges and boosters, which calibration teaches learners to deploy deliberately
Evaluating others' work in academic prose relies on choosing reporting verbs by their evaluative force
Evaluating sources applies general evaluation skills — criteria, strengths and weaknesses, judgement — to other scholars' work
A distinct authorial voice depends on keeping the writer's own averrals separate from, and in control of, attributed content
Self-mention is one of the most visible resources through which writers construct authorial presence
Voice is projected through the degree of commitment writers attach to their claims
Exemplification markers are the code glosses learners meet first; reformulation and reader-oriented glossing build on them
Correct use of i.e., e.g. and viz. as glossing devices depends on knowing what these abbreviations mean
The concept of graded commitment learned through hedging transfers to spoken stance, although the devices differ
Spoken stance uses different resources (opinion frames, vague language, prosody) from writing, so awareness of spoken–written differences prevents transfer of written hedges into talk

guidance.summary: Halliday and Hasan give teachers a precise vocabulary for cohesive ties, but their own account treats cohesion as only one condition of a text hanging together, alongside consistency with its context. Crossley and McNamara found that computational indices of explicit local cohesion did not predict higher human ratings of L2 essays, whereas indices of linguistic sophistication did, which supports teaching coherence as a matter of ordered ideas and reader expectations with devices in a supporting role. Begin from readers' experience (where did you lose the thread?) before naming devices.

activities.title: Connector-stripping test
learnerActions: Read a well-organised model paragraph from which all connectors have been removed
Mark each sentence boundary where the relation is still clear and each where it is not
Reinsert connectors only where a relation was unclear, then compare with the original
activities.intendedInsight: Much of a text's coherence is carried by order, repetition and topic continuity; connectors are needed only at certain junctures.
activities.rationale: Makes the cohesion/coherence distinction experiential and directly challenges the assumption that more devices mean better organisation, an assumption at odds with findings on cohesion indices and rated quality.

activities.title: Where did I lose the thread?
learnerActions: Read a partner's paragraph and mark every point at which you had to pause to work out the connection
Discuss each mark and classify it as a tie problem (unclear reference, wrong connector) or a coherence problem (missing step, off-topic sentence)
Revise your own paragraph in light of your partner's marks
activities.intendedInsight: Readers' difficulties have different causes, and only some are solved by adding linking words.
activities.rationale: Hoey models written text as an interaction in which the reader's implicit questions must be answered; peer reading makes those questions visible to the writer.

difficulties.pattern: 'My feedback said cohesion, so I added Furthermore and Moreover to more sentences.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Connectors at the start of most sentences, often mismatched to the actual relation, while underlying problems of order or relevance remain.
difficulties.response: Show what the feedback was pointing to by tracing the reader's path through the text; ask the learner to name the relation each connector signals. Do not respond by banning connectors, which simply transfers the problem.

difficulties.pattern: 'All my sentences are about climate change, so the paragraph is coherent.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that list related facts on one topic with no controlling point and no progression from one sentence to the next.
difficulties.response: Have the learner write a one-line function for each sentence (claim, reason, example, consequence) and check whether each advances the paragraph's point; distinguish topic from point.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a six-sentence paragraph in which sentence four introduces an unrelated point but is linked by 'Moreover', and comments on how well the paragraph hangs together.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies sentence four as breaking the paragraph's logical unity despite the connector, explains that a connector signals but cannot create a relation, and proposes moving or cutting the sentence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a problem but attributes it to the choice of connector and proposes a different one.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Judges the paragraph well organised because it uses linking words.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, introduce the distinction through reader experience and simple paragraph models without heavy terminology. On pre-sessional courses, connect it to marking criteria that separate coherence from cohesion and to reverse outlining. In undergraduate in-sessional work it is most useful diagnostically, in tutorials on students' own drafts.
reviewNotes: The Crossley and McNamara finding derives from automated indices applied to a particular L2 essay corpus; it supports caution about equating device counts with quality rather than any claim that cohesion is irrelevant.

guidance.summary: Halliday and Hasan's categories of reiteration (repetition, synonym, superordinate, general word) and collocation, together with reference, give learners a toolkit for analysing how expert texts keep participants in view. Thompson offers an accessible functional account suitable for teacher explanation. Chain-tracing on authentic disciplinary paragraphs shows that key nouns are repeated far more than school advice about avoiding repetition implies, and that article choice often signals second mention.

activities.title: Colour the chains
learnerActions: Take a paragraph from a textbook or article in your field and highlight every expression referring to each main participant in a different colour
Count how often each participant is repeated, pronominalised, replaced by a synonym or referred to with a general noun
Compare counts with a partner from a different discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Expert writers repeat key nouns frequently and use pronouns mainly where the antecedent is unmistakable.
activities.rationale: Visual analysis promotes noticing of a pattern learners tend to underestimate; noticing is widely argued to be a condition for uptake.

activities.title: Repair the referent
learnerActions: Revise a learner-style paragraph that contains ambiguous it/they and a drifting synonym chain
Justify each change to a partner by stating what the reader would otherwise have assumed
activities.intendedInsight: Changing the word for a referent is a meaning choice, not a stylistic decoration.
activities.rationale: Working on plausible learner text targets the repair skill needed for self-editing and links reference choices to reader inference.

difficulties.pattern: 'I was taught never to repeat a word, so I change it every time.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Synonym cycling (participants, subjects, people, individuals) that leads readers to wonder whether different groups are meant.
difficulties.response: Show textbook or corpus evidence of repetition of key nouns; distinguish variation in non-technical wording from fixed reference to key participants. Avoid replacing one blanket rule with another ('always repeat').

difficulties.pattern: Second mention with 'a' or no article, or omitted subject pronouns, so that chains break down.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'A participant… A participant said…' for the same person; missing 'it' as subject; readers unsure whether a new entity is introduced.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages lack articles or allow null subjects benefit from focused work on first versus subsequent mention, using the learner's own texts as data.

difficulties.pattern: 'It' or 'they' placed after several intervening nouns in long sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers cannot resolve the pronoun without rereading; peer readers propose different antecedents.
