difficulties.response: Teach a simple check: if two candidate antecedents exist, repeat the noun or use a precise general noun.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes three linked sentences about a process or study in their field and underlines every expression referring to the main participant.
diagnostic.strongResponse: The chain mixes repetition, pronoun and a general noun; every reference is resolvable; articles shift appropriately from first to second mention.
diagnostic.partialResponse: The chain is resolvable but relies on a single device (only pronouns or only repetition), or contains one article slip.
diagnostic.gapResponse: The referent shifts or is ambiguous; synonyms imply different entities.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on pronoun and article reference and simple repetition in textbook paragraphs. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work extends to general nouns and the risks of synonym substitution in source-based writing. For taught postgraduates the emphasis moves to longer chains across sections and to disciplinary expectations about repeating technical terms.
reviewNotes: The claim that expert prose repeats key nouns more than learners expect is a teaching generalisation consistent with corpus descriptions; it is not quantified here for particular disciplines.

guidance.summary: Biber et al. describe the semantic categories of linking adverbials and show that a relatively small set accounts for most uses in academic prose. Learner-corpus studies, including Altenberg and Tapper's chapter in Granger's collection and Granger and Tyson's comparison of native and non-native student essays, report overuse of some connectors, underuse of others and sentence-initial stacking relative to first-language student essays (comparisons that measure difference from a reference corpus rather than error, so expert disciplinary writing is the better model); Hinkel similarly documents L2 writers' reliance on sentence-level transitions. Teach connectors by relation and with evidence of expert frequency, aiming for fewer, better-chosen links rather than long lists of supposed equivalents.

activities.title: Frequency reality check
learnerActions: Count linking adverbials per 100 words in a paragraph of your own and in a published paragraph from your field
Note their positions (initial, medial) and the relations they signal
Delete connectors from your paragraph wherever the relation is already clear, and reread
activities.intendedInsight: Expert prose uses fewer connectors, places some medially and relies on content to carry many relations.
activities.rationale: Self-comparison with expert texts targets the overuse and sentence-initial stacking documented in learner corpora.

activities.title: Relation first, connector second
learnerActions: For each of ten sentence pairs, decide the relation (addition, contrast, concession, result, exemplification) before choosing any connector
Choose a connector or decide that none is needed
Discuss pairs where the group chose no connector
activities.intendedInsight: A connector should follow from a judged relation, and sometimes the best choice is none.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Hasan's grouping of conjunctive relations into additive, adversative, causal and temporal gives learners a manageable framework for the prior judgement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Every sentence should start with a linking word to show cohesion.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Chains such as Firstly… Secondly… Moreover… Furthermore… In addition… with a connector before most sentences.
difficulties.response: Show expert density and ask learners to justify each connector by naming the relation. Do not ban connectors or impose an arbitrary quota.

difficulties.pattern: Treating connectors from a list as interchangeable, for example 'On the other hand' to add a point.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'On the other hand' with no preceding contrast; 'Besides' as a neutral additive in formal writing.
difficulties.response: Teach connectors grouped by relation and register with authentic examples, and return to mismatches in the learner's own text.

difficulties.pattern: Using 'however' like 'but' to join two clauses with a comma.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comma splices of the form '…, however, …' between independent clauses.
difficulties.response: Contrast 'but' (coordinator), 'although' (subordinator) and 'however' (adverbial) with the same content, and show the punctuation each requires.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites a 100-word paragraph in which five of six sentences begin with a connector, keeping only the links a reader needs.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Keeps two or three connectors that mark genuine contrast or result, removes additive stacking, moves at least one connector medially and punctuates correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Removes some connectors but keeps mismatched ones or retains sentence-initial positioning throughout.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Replaces connectors with different connectors, keeping the density unchanged.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need the core semantic categories and punctuation. Pre-sessional courses should explicitly address test-preparation habits of connector stacking. Undergraduate in-sessional support works best on students' own assignments, where connector overuse often masks problems of argument structure.
reviewNotes: Hinkel (2002) reports frequencies across specific L1 groups and essay prompts; verify feature labels before quoting figures to teachers.
grangertyson1996 is a proposed reference; the supporting claim is also attributed to the Granger (1998) collection.

guidance.summary: Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman treat logical connectors by both semantic class and grammatical type, which is the combination learners need: what relation is meant, and what syntax follows. Biber et al. provide frequency and positional evidence, and learner-corpus studies show that common errors involve mismatch rather than absence of connectors. Teach through minimal pairs that make the change in claim visible, and through the consequences of an unjustified 'therefore' for the argument.

activities.title: Minimal pairs
learnerActions: Read two versions of a sentence pair that differ only in the connector (however versus on the contrary; whereas versus although)
Paraphrase the claim each version makes
Decide which version the writer most plausibly intended given the surrounding text
activities.intendedInsight: Connectors change propositions, not just style.
activities.rationale: Contrasting forms in controlled pairs focuses attention on meaning differences that are easily blurred in lists.

activities.title: Concordance check: therefore, thus, hence
learnerActions: Examine prepared concordance lines from an academic corpus for therefore, thus and hence
Record typical positions and what follows each (for example thus + -ing clause)
Rewrite three of your own sentences using the pattern you found
activities.intendedInsight: Near-synonymous resultative connectors have distinct grammatical and positional preferences.
activities.rationale: Corpus consultation lets learners discover usage patterns directly; meta-analytic evidence suggests data-driven learning can be effective, though effects vary with design.

difficulties.pattern: 'Although the sample was small, but the results were clear.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Double marking of concession with although…but or though…yet.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages mark both clauses of a concessive construction need to see that English marks only one; contrast the two English options with the same content.

difficulties.pattern: 'On the contrary' used for simple contrast between two entities.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'X is expensive. On the contrary, Y is cheap.'
difficulties.response: Teach 'on the contrary' as rejecting a preceding (often negated) proposition, and 'in contrast' for comparing two items.

difficulties.pattern: 'Therefore' introducing a conclusion the preceding sentences do not support.
difficulties.revealedBy: A list of facts followed by 'Therefore,…' with no warrant connecting them to the claim.
difficulties.response: Ask 'why does this follow?' and have the learner write the missing step; treat the connector as a promise the content must keep.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains the difference between 'Sales fell. However, profits rose.' and 'Sales did not fall. On the contrary, they rose.' and writes one sentence with 'whereas' comparing two methods.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies contrast versus correction of a negated claim, and produces a well-formed 'whereas' sentence comparing two parallel items.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a difference but cannot name it, or misuses 'whereas' as a sentence-initial adverbial.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats the connectors as interchangeable.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses this topic is best integrated with argument writing and feedback on learners' own texts. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support can tie precision to disciplinary reasoning, for example inference in quantitative fields or concession in humanities argument.

guidance.summary: Systemic functional accounts distinguish theme–rheme (the clause's point of departure) from given–new (what the reader is assumed to know), which typically but not always coincide. For EAP, Swales and Feak's advice on old-to-new information flow offers a practical entry point, and Thompson explains the systems accessibly. The passive is best taught here as a tool for arranging information rather than as a marker of objectivity, and work should use sentence pairs so that 'given' is always relative to preceding text.

activities.title: Which version follows?
learnerActions: Read sentence 1 of a short passage, then choose between an active and a passive version of sentence 2
Explain your choice by pointing to what sentence 1 has already introduced
Repeat with a different sentence 1 that reverses the best choice
activities.intendedInsight: Voice and subject choice depend on context; neither active nor passive is better in itself.
activities.rationale: Directly counters the myth that the passive is inherently more objective or academic, and shows information flow as the reason for the choice.

activities.title: Old-to-new audit
learnerActions: Underline the first noun phrase of each sentence in your own paragraph
Check whether it links back to something already mentioned
Rewrite any sentence that opens with brand-new information
activities.intendedInsight: Many 'choppy' paragraphs open sentences with new information.
activities.rationale: Applying the principle to one's own text builds a self-editing routine rather than abstract knowledge.

difficulties.pattern: 'The passive is more academic, so I use it whenever I can.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive sentences that place new information first and push given information to the end.
difficulties.response: Show pairs where the active is the better choice because of what precedes it. Do not replace this with 'avoid the passive'.

difficulties.pattern: Fronting a topic and then repeating it with a pronoun: 'This problem, researchers have studied it for decades.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dislocated topics with resumptive pronouns; unusual word order at the start of clauses.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages mark topic through word order or particles benefit from seeing the English resources for the same purpose: passive, a different subject, existential there or a summarising noun phrase.

difficulties.pattern: Very long subjects carrying new information before the main verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers wait a long time for the verb; heavy noun phrases at the start of clauses.
difficulties.response: Show how moving the heavy, new element to the end (end-weight) improves processing; link to sentence-level editing.

diagnostic.task: The learner improves the flow of: 'Rising sea levels threaten coastal cities. Large-scale relocation programmes may be required by this threat.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Rewrites so that 'This threat' opens sentence two (This threat may require…) and explains that it links back to the previous sentence.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves the sentence but cannot explain why the new version reads better.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the order unchanged or makes only lexical changes.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce the principle through sentence pairs and short paragraphs. In undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support it becomes a revision tool for students' own drafts. Doctoral writers benefit from applying it to dense methods and discussion prose, where long subjects are common.

guidance.summary: Daneš's typology of thematic progression gives a compact model learners can apply to their own drafts, and Thompson's functional grammar explains theme without heavy terminology. Halliday and Martin show how scientific writing nominalises the rheme of one clause so that it can serve as the theme of the next, building chains of reasoning — a pattern worth making explicit to writers in all fields. Present the patterns as diagnostic tools rather than templates: expert paragraphs mix them.

activities.title: Theme arrows on your own draft
learnerActions: Mark the theme of each sentence in a paragraph you have written
Draw an arrow from each theme to the earlier theme or rheme it picks up
Revise any sentence whose theme has no arrow
activities.intendedInsight: Disjointed paragraphs often contain themes that do not connect to anything earlier.
activities.rationale: Daneš's patterns become a practical revision check when applied to learners' own writing rather than only to model texts.

activities.title: Nominalise to move on
learnerActions: For each sentence pair, turn the process described in sentence 1 into a noun phrase that can open sentence 2 (Temperatures rose → This rise…)
Compare the result with a version that uses bare 'This' or 'It'
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalisation lets a writer carry a whole process forward as the starting point of the next step.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin identify this rheme-to-theme nominalisation as central to how scientific argument is built.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study… The study… It… The study…' — the same theme throughout a paragraph that should develop an argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: List-like paragraphs in which each sentence adds a fact about the same participant without building a line of reasoning.
difficulties.response: Show how linear progression lets each sentence build on the last. Do not tell learners to vary the subject with synonyms, which damages reference.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing theme with topic, or treating a fronted adverbial as the whole theme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent analysis of themes in exercises; uncertainty about what counts as the theme.
difficulties.response: Use an operational teaching definition (everything up to and including the subject) and acknowledge it as a simplification of the grammatical account.

difficulties.pattern: Nominalising every process to create linear progression, producing dense, opaque sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of abstract nouns with weak verbs (the implementation of the improvement of…).
difficulties.response: Treat nominalisation as a resource with costs for clarity; use it at the point of linkage, not throughout.

diagnostic.task: The learner analyses the themes in a five-sentence published paragraph, names the dominant pattern and identifies one sentence that would be harder to follow if its theme were changed.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels themes accurately, recognises a mix of linear and derived progression and explains the link that a changed theme would break.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Labels most themes but cannot relate them to the progression patterns or explain their effect.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify themes consistently or sees no connection between successive sentence openings.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses keep terminology light and focus on arrows and linking. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support can use the patterns to diagnose paragraphs in assignments and dissertations. Doctoral writers often respond well to the full model when revising dense theoretical or methods prose.

guidance.summary: Flowerdew's work on signalling nouns shows how nouns such as problem, process and aspect take specific meaning from co-text, both anaphorically and cataphorically. Swales and Feak's 'this + summary word' advice gives a teachable rule of thumb, while corpus work on this and these in published prose suggests that bare 'this' also occurs, so the issue is reader clarity rather than an absolute ban. Teach labels as choices that categorise and evaluate as well as link.

activities.title: Label the shell
learnerActions: Find every this/these/such + noun in a research article extract
Bracket the stretch of text each one encapsulates
Decide whether the noun also evaluates (claim, assertion, problem) and how
activities.intendedInsight: Signalling nouns both summarise and classify what came before, often with an evaluative angle.
activities.rationale: Flowerdew's analysis shows that the meaning of these nouns is realised in co-text, so learners need to see the stretch being encapsulated.

activities.title: Upgrade the bare 'this'
learnerActions: Search your draft for sentence-initial This and It
Decide for each whether a reader could misidentify the referent
Add a precise noun where needed and compare two alternative labels for their effect
activities.intendedInsight: Adding a noun clarifies reference and lets the writer characterise the previous content.
activities.rationale: A search-and-revise routine converts a known rule of thumb into a self-editing habit.

difficulties.pattern: 'This shows that…' where 'this' could refer to several preceding ideas.
difficulties.revealedBy: Readers ask 'this what?'; peers bracket different antecedents.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to name what 'this' refers to; if it takes more than a word or two to say, add a signalling noun.

difficulties.pattern: A narrow repertoire: 'this issue', 'this problem', 'this thing' for every kind of content.
difficulties.revealedBy: The same two or three labels used for findings, arguments, methods and proposals alike.
difficulties.response: Build a sorted bank of signalling nouns from reading in the learner's field (finding, trend, assumption, limitation, distinction).

difficulties.pattern: Inadvertent evaluation, such as calling a well-supported result 'this claim' or 'this assumption'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Labels that undercut the writer's own or a source's position without the writer intending it.
difficulties.response: Compare the effect of finding, claim, assertion and assumption on the same content and discuss the stance each implies.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads two sentences reporting a study's result and continues with a sentence beginning 'This ___ suggests…'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Supplies an accurate label (result, finding, pattern) and can explain why 'claim' or 'assumption' would change the stance.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Supplies a plausible but vague label (issue, situation).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves 'This' bare or chooses a label that misrepresents the content.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can introduce 'this + noun' as a high-yield revision habit. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support should extend to cataphoric uses and evaluative labelling in literature reviews. Doctoral writers benefit from attention to how labelling positions others' work.
reviewNotes: graycortes2011 is a proposed reference; if it cannot be verified, the statement that bare 'this' occurs in published prose should be supported from another corpus source or softened.

guidance.summary: Hoey's accounts of culturally popular text patterns, building on Winter's clause relations, show that readers recognise patterns through lexical signals and that patterns can be recursive, as when a negatively evaluated response creates a new problem. Carrell found that explicit training in top-level rhetorical structure improved ESL readers' recall, supporting the teaching of patterns for reading as well as writing. Swales and Feak's units on general–specific and problem–process–solution texts provide graduate-level writing models.

activities.title: Signal hunt
learnerActions: Highlight the problem, response and evaluation vocabulary in a problem–solution passage
Map the passage onto situation–problem–response–evaluation boxes
Find any point where a negative evaluation triggers a further problem and response
activities.intendedInsight: Patterns are signalled lexically and can repeat within one text.
activities.rationale: Hoey shows that readers rely on lexical signals to recognise pattern elements; making signals explicit builds this recognition.

activities.title: Predict the next paragraph
learnerActions: Read a text paragraph by paragraph with the remainder covered
Before uncovering each paragraph, predict its function from the pattern so far
Compare predictions with the original and discuss the signals that helped
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing the pattern lets readers anticipate content and read more efficiently.
activities.rationale: Carrell's study of ESL readers found that training in text structure improved recall, which suggests pattern awareness supports comprehension.

difficulties.pattern: Treating patterns as fixed templates and forcing every task into problem–solution.
difficulties.revealedBy: A compare-and-contrast task answered as a problem–solution essay; artificial 'problems' invented to fit the frame.
difficulties.response: Present patterns as reader expectations that the task and content select, and practise matching tasks to patterns.

difficulties.pattern: Responses listed without any evaluation, so the pattern stops short.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that describe several solutions but never assess whether they work.
difficulties.response: Show that evaluation is an expected element; ask 'did it work, and how do we know?' after each response.

difficulties.pattern: Reading a reported view in a claim–counterclaim structure as the writer's own position.
difficulties.revealedBy: Summaries that attribute to the writer a view the writer goes on to reject.
difficulties.response: Teach the signals of the hypothetical element (it is often claimed, many assume) and the real element (in fact, however, the evidence suggests).

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 200-word passage and labels its pattern elements, then writes one sentence that would continue the pattern.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Labels elements correctly with reference to signals, and the continuation fits the next expected element (for example an evaluation of the response).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the overall pattern but mislabels one element or writes a continuation that repeats an earlier element.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the content without recognising any organising pattern.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, use simple problem–solution and general–specific texts from subject textbooks for both reading and writing. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses can add claim–counterclaim structures, which are important for following argument. Taught postgraduates benefit from using patterns to read research articles and policy documents efficiently.
reviewNotes: Carrell (1985) used Meyer's top-level structures rather than Hoey's patterns; the two frameworks overlap but are not identical, so the evidence supports pattern awareness in general rather than Hoey's taxonomy specifically.

guidance.summary: In Hyland's interpersonal model, frame markers are one category of interactive metadiscourse; Hyland and Tse's study of postgraduate dissertations shows metadiscourse use varying by discipline and by degree level. Bunton's analysis of PhD thesis introductions identifies outlining the structure of the thesis as a regular element. Teach density relative to genre and length: roadmaps that suit a thesis can read as mechanical in a short essay, and propositional signposting (what a section shows) is more useful than procedural announcement (what it talks about).

activities.title: Roadmap scaling
learnerActions: Compare roadmap sentences from a short essay, a dissertation chapter and a research article
Note how much each previews and how it is worded
Write a roadmap for your current assignment at the appropriate scale
activities.intendedInsight: The amount and form of signposting should match the length and genre of the text.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence of variation across disciplines and levels supports teaching metadiscourse as genre-sensitive rather than as a fixed formula.

activities.title: Metatext audit
learnerActions: Highlight all metatext in your draft
Delete any that does not help a reader navigate
Rewrite procedural metatext as propositional signposting
activities.intendedInsight: Useful frame markers tell readers what a part of the text establishes, not only what it is about.
activities.rationale: Treating frame markers as reader-oriented metadiscourse focuses revision on their function for the reader.

difficulties.pattern: 'This essay will discuss X, Y and Z' followed by 'In this paragraph I will…' at the start of every paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Formulaic roadmaps and paragraph-level announcements in short essays.
difficulties.response: Show propositional roadmaps that preview the argument; reserve paragraph-level metatext for long texts. Do not ban 'This essay will', which is acceptable in many contexts.

difficulties.pattern: A roadmap that no longer matches the body after revision.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sections appear in a different order from the one promised, or a promised section is missing.
difficulties.response: Encourage writing or revising the roadmap last and checking it against a reverse outline.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly as the only structure for a complex argument.
difficulties.revealedBy: Enumerated points of unequal weight with no indication of how they relate.
difficulties.response: Show how stage labels and topic shifts can signal relations (more importantly, a further complication) as well as order.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites the sentence 'This essay will talk about the causes, effects and solutions of urban flooding.' as a roadmap for a 2,500-word argumentative essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a roadmap that previews the argument and its stages (for example, argues that drainage policy matters more than climate factors, first by…), at an appropriate length.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Improves register but still lists topics without signalling the argument.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Retains a topic list or adds paragraph-by-paragraph announcements.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners need simple, accurate roadmaps for short essays and reports. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work should address scaling for dissertations. Doctoral writers need chapter-level metatext across a thesis, which links to thesis macrostructure.

guidance.summary: Transitions are where coherence at text level becomes visible to the reader. Wingate's work on students' understanding of argument identifies the coherent presentation of a position across a text as a component many students do not recognise, and Hoey's view of text as interaction suggests that a paragraph opening should answer the reader's question 'how does this relate to what I just read?'. Teach transitions through reverse outlining of paragraph relations and through encapsulation with signalling nouns, rather than through inventories of 'transition words'.

activities.title: Relation map
learnerActions: Write a one-line summary of each paragraph in your draft
Label the relation between each pair of consecutive paragraphs (extends, contrasts, qualifies, applies, results from)
Rewrite each paragraph opening so that it expresses that relation
activities.intendedInsight: Paragraph relations should be stated where the reader needs them — at the opening of the new paragraph.
activities.rationale: Making the argument's structure explicit addresses the component of argument Wingate found students often overlook.

activities.title: Bridge building
learnerActions: Read pairs of paragraph endings and beginnings joined only by 'Furthermore'
Replace each with a bridging sentence that encapsulates the previous point and introduces the new one
Compare versions and discuss which shows the argument more clearly
activities.intendedInsight: A summarising noun phrase plus the new point does more work than a bare connector.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's advice on linking ideas with summary words gives a concrete technique for bridging.

difficulties.pattern: 'Another reason is… Another reason is… Another reason is…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs added in sequence with no indication of how they relate or build.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to rank the points and decide which depends on which, then write openings that reflect that structure.

difficulties.pattern: Paragraph-initial 'Furthermore' or 'Moreover' used as the transition regardless of relation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Additive connectors opening paragraphs that actually contrast with or qualify the previous one.
difficulties.response: Show encapsulating openings and ask learners to state the relation in words before choosing any connector.

difficulties.pattern: Transitions written before paragraphs were reordered, so bridges no longer fit.
difficulties.revealedBy: Openings that refer back to points that now come later or have been cut.
difficulties.response: Add a final check of every paragraph opening after any structural revision.

diagnostic.task: The learner is given two consecutive paragraph summaries (Paragraph A: cost explains part of a decline; Paragraph B: changing consumer attitudes) and writes the opening of Paragraph B.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a bridging sentence that encapsulates A and positions B in relation to it (While cost explains part of the decline, it cannot account for…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Introduces B clearly but links to A only with a connector (In addition, attitudes…).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Begins B with no reference to A.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should introduce relational transitions in extended essays. Undergraduate in-sessional work can use students' assignments for reverse outlining. Taught postgraduate support extends to transitions between dissertation sections and chapters.

guidance.summary: Halliday and Martin show that technical terms in science form taxonomies, so a change of term can imply a different place in the taxonomy; Hyland and Tse show that apparently general academic words take discipline-specific meanings. Both point to the same teaching message: in academic writing, lexical variation carries meaning. Address the prior-schooling expectation that repetition is poor style, and give learners a concrete self-editing routine.

activities.title: Term inventory
learnerActions: List the five most important concepts in your draft
Use find-all to locate every expression you used for each
Standardise wherever variants refer to the same concept, and add an explicit note where a distinct term is intended
activities.intendedInsight: Many apparent synonyms in one's own text turn out to be unintended variation.
activities.rationale: Repetition is itself a cohesive device; a mechanical search turns this principle into a reliable editing habit.

activities.title: Same or different?
learnerActions: In discipline groups, judge pairs of terms from your field (for example sex and gender; effect and impact; learner autonomy and self-directed learning)
Check how glossaries or key sources in the field distinguish them
Report one pair that the field treats as distinct and one it treats as interchangeable
activities.intendedInsight: Whether two terms are interchangeable is a disciplinary question, not a dictionary one.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse's evidence on discipline-specific meaning and Halliday and Martin's account of technical taxonomies both support discipline-based judgement.

difficulties.pattern: 'Repeating the same word is boring, so I use synonyms.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Key concepts referred to by three or four different terms; readers or markers asking whether a new concept has been introduced.
difficulties.response: Show published texts that repeat key terms; distinguish variation in everyday wording from fixed technical reference.

difficulties.pattern: One concept rendered by different English terms in different sections.
difficulties.revealedBy: Inconsistent English equivalents for one source-language term, especially when drafting through the first language or machine translation.
difficulties.response: Encourage a personal bilingual term list for each project and a final find-all consistency check.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding pronouns and general nouns altogether to stay 'consistent'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mechanical repetition of long noun phrases where a pronoun or 'this approach' would be clear.
difficulties.response: Clarify that consistency applies to the naming of concepts, not to banning reference devices.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 200-word paragraph that uses 'motivation', 'drive', 'willingness' and 'engagement' for the same construct, and comments on it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the variation, explains that a reader in the field might take these as distinct constructs, and standardises with a justification.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices variation but considers it acceptable style, or standardises without explaining why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees no issue, or praises the variety of vocabulary.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce the principle with extended source-based writing. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support should link it to disciplinary terminology and dissertation editing. Doctoral writers need consistency across chapters, publications and figures, often for a large set of defined constructs.

guidance.summary: Hinds proposed reader versus writer responsibility as a dimension of variation between writing traditions; later intercultural rhetoric (Connor) and critical contrastive rhetoric (Kubota and Lehner) caution against treating such typologies as fixed national or cultural traits. Teach the concept as an explicit statement of a tacit expectation among many anglophone markers, framed as a convention to manage rather than a deficit to correct. Biber and Gray's evidence that academic prose leaves many relations implicit within compressed noun phrases is a useful counterweight: explicitness is selective even in English.

activities.title: Where would a reader stop?
learnerActions: Read a partner's paragraph aloud and pause wherever you have to infer a connection
The writer notes each pause and decides whether to state the connection
Discuss which inferences an expert reader in the field could reasonably be expected to make
activities.intendedInsight: How much to make explicit depends on the reader, but many markers expect key links to be stated.
activities.rationale: Turns Hinds's abstract typology into a concrete, reader-based judgement about a specific text.

activities.title: Comparing traditions without stereotypes
learnerActions: Bring a short academic text from another language you know or from a different discipline
Identify where its main point and key links are made explicit (title, opening, headings, conclusion)
Discuss the variation you find within each language as well as between them
activities.intendedInsight: Explicitness conventions vary by genre and discipline as well as by language, and no tradition is uniform.
activities.rationale: Draws on learners' plurilingual resources while reflecting intercultural and critical critiques of contrastive generalisations.

difficulties.pattern: 'I build up to my main point so that the conclusion has more impact.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Main claims withheld until the conclusion or left implicit; feedback such as 'what is your argument?'.
difficulties.response: Writers whose previous schooling rewarded delayed or implied conclusions can be shown the genre expectation and asked to compare effects for the target reader, without implying their earlier practice was wrong.

difficulties.pattern: 'Changing how I write means my previous writing was bad.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Resistance to feedback on explicitness; discomfort when discussing other writing traditions.
difficulties.response: Frame the topic as expanding a repertoire for different readers rather than replacing a deficient habit.

difficulties.pattern: Over-explicitness after instruction: stating the obvious and narrating every step.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy metatext and explanations of points an expert reader would take for granted.
difficulties.response: Return to the intended reader: explicitness is about the links that matter to the argument, not about everything.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains in their own words why a UK tutor might write 'make your argument explicit' on an essay whose main point appears only in the conclusion.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains the expectation that the writer states the position and links early and clearly, and notes that this is a convention of the context rather than a universal rule.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Explains the expectation but presents it as the only logical way to write.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot connect the comment to explicitness, or interprets it as a grammar issue.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation and pre-sessional level the concept is useful for interpreting feedback and for introductions and topic sentences. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support can address it in tutorials when students are puzzled by comments on clarity. Handle it with care in multilingual groups to avoid stereotyping.
reviewNotes: Hinds's typology is contested; the topic name is retained from the skeleton, but teachers should present it as a heuristic about reader expectations rather than as a description of national writing styles.

guidance.summary: Chaudron and Richards found that macro-markers aided lecture comprehension more than micro-markers alone; Thompson showed that lecturers also signal organisation through intonation and that EAP listening materials do not always reflect authentic structuring patterns. Biber, Conrad and Cortes found discourse-organising lexical bundles particularly frequent in classroom teaching, and Young's analysis of lecture phases offers a frame for what markers signal. Teach from authentic or authentic-like recordings, combining reception and production and attending to prosody.

activities.title: Lecture skeleton from markers
learnerActions: Listen to a lecture extract and log every phrase that signals a change of topic or phase
Use the log to reconstruct an outline of the lecture
Compare outlines and discuss boundaries signalled only by pause or pitch
activities.intendedInsight: Macro-markers and prosody give listeners the structure they cannot see.
activities.rationale: Chaudron and Richards's finding on macro-markers and Young's phase model both suggest that attention to structuring language supports lecture comprehension.

activities.title: Written-to-spoken swap
learnerActions: Take a written paragraph that uses Furthermore and Moreover
Turn it into a one-minute spoken explanation using spoken markers and pauses
Record it, listen back and note where a listener might get lost
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken signposting is worded and paced differently from written linking.
activities.rationale: Biber, Conrad and Cortes show that classroom teaching uses distinctive discourse-organising bundles, and Thompson highlights the role of intonation in signalling organisation.

difficulties.pattern: Hearing 'so' or 'OK' as a signal that the lecture is concluding.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes that stop recording after a micro-marker; learners missing the main point that follows.
difficulties.response: Show the range of functions of micro-markers in authentic transcripts and contrast them with macro-markers that do signal conclusion.

difficulties.pattern: Presentations that sound read aloud because they use written connectors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Furthermore, Moreover and In addition in spoken presentations; listeners losing the structure.
difficulties.response: Model spoken markers and rehearse them as chunks; draw attention to differences between spoken and written registers.

difficulties.pattern: Markers planned in advance disappear under the pressure of live delivery.
difficulties.revealedBy: Presentations with clear slides but no verbal signalling between sections.
difficulties.response: Rehearse transitions specifically and attach them to slide changes; avoid scripting entire talks.

diagnostic.task: The learner listens to a two-minute lecture extract and writes down the phrase that marks each new section, then gives a 30-second spoken preview of a topic of their choice.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies all section boundaries with their markers, and produces a natural spoken preview with at least two macro-markers and a pause at the boundary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies most boundaries but misses one marked only by prosody, or produces a preview in written style.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot identify boundaries; the preview lacks any structuring language.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses emphasise recognition in lectures alongside short presentations. Undergraduate in-sessional work concentrates on assessed presentations and seminar contributions. Taught postgraduate and doctoral learners need signposting for longer research presentations and, for doctoral students who teach, for their own lecturing.

guidance.summary: Trimble identifies definition as a core rhetorical function of scientific and technical discourse, distinguishing formal and less formal definitions and ways of expanding them. Swales and Feak show how graduate writers use definitions to display knowledge and position themselves, including by engaging with contested definitions, and Halliday and Martin show that technical definitions build taxonomies in science. Teach the formal definition frame early, then move quickly to definitions in authentic disciplinary use.

activities.title: Class and difference
learnerActions: Write formal definitions of three terms from your field (term, class, distinguishing features)
Test each by asking whether another term from the same class would also fit the definition
Add or sharpen distinguishing features until only your term fits
activities.intendedInsight: A definition works only if its distinguishing features exclude other members of the class.
activities.rationale: Trimble's account of formal definition gives a clear structure; the substitution test makes its logic operational.

activities.title: Whose definition?
learnerActions: Collect two or three definitions of a contested term from sources in your field
Note what each includes and excludes
Write a short paragraph presenting the definitions and stating which one you adopt and why
activities.intendedInsight: In many fields definition is an argument, and choosing a definition is part of the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's treatment of definitions in graduate writing emphasises their role in positioning the writer.

difficulties.pattern: 'Globalisation is the process of globalising the world.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Circular definitions or definitions with no class word; relative clauses that do not attach to a class.
difficulties.response: Practise the term–class–features frame with the defining relative clause, using the learner's own terms.

difficulties.pattern: 'The Oxford Dictionary defines culture as…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Essays opening with general-dictionary definitions where a disciplinary definition is expected.
difficulties.response: Show how sources in the field define the term and discuss why a general dictionary rarely captures disciplinary meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Treating a contested term as having one correct definition.
difficulties.revealedBy: A single definition presented without attribution for terms such as 'identity' or 'sustainability'.
difficulties.response: Present competing definitions and require an explicit adoption statement.

diagnostic.task: The learner defines 'renewable energy' (or a key term in their field) in one sentence and then states whether the term is contested.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a formal definition with class and distinguishing features and recognises where definitions in the field differ.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a usable definition without a clear class word, or does not recognise contestation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives a circular or example-only definition.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on formal definitions of subject terms in textbooks and short-answer questions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses add extended and source-based definitions. Taught postgraduate students need operational and contested definitions in dissertations.

guidance.summary: Trimble treats classification as a core function of scientific and technical discourse, and Mohan's knowledge framework places classification among the knowledge structures that link language and content. In Rose and Martin's genre map, classifying reports are a recognised factual genre. Teach classification through visual organisers (tree diagrams) and then prose, and push beyond formulae to the criterion and its limits, which is where academic value lies.

activities.title: Tree to text and back
learnerActions: Describe a classification tree diagram in a paragraph
Give your paragraph to a partner who redraws the tree without seeing the original
Compare the trees and revise the paragraph where they differ
activities.intendedInsight: Clear classification prose lets a reader reconstruct the scheme exactly.
activities.rationale: Mohan's knowledge framework links knowledge structures to graphic organisers and to language, supporting movement between diagram and text.

activities.title: Spot the faulty scheme
learnerActions: Examine classifications that mix criteria or leave out categories
Identify the problem in each
Repair one scheme and state its basis explicitly
activities.intendedInsight: Classification depends on a single, explicit criterion.
activities.rationale: Trimble's treatment of classification stresses the basis of classification as part of the function.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing criteria within one scheme (vehicles divided into cars, electric vehicles and red vehicles).
difficulties.revealedBy: Overlapping categories; items that fit more than one category.
difficulties.response: Require learners to state the criterion before listing categories and to test each category against it.

difficulties.pattern: 'The system is consisted of three parts' or 'comprises of three parts'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive forms of consist of; comprise followed by of.
difficulties.response: Contrast consist of (active only), comprise (no 'of') and be composed of (passive), with corpus examples.

difficulties.pattern: Listing members without naming the categories or the scheme.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lists of examples with no superordinate terms.
difficulties.response: Return to class words and practise naming categories before giving members.

diagnostic.task: The learner classifies a list of ten items from their field and writes two sentences describing the classification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Groups items by one stated criterion, names the categories and uses classification verbs accurately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Groups items sensibly but does not state the criterion or makes a verb error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Groups inconsistently or lists items without categories.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes use classification extensively in science, engineering and business content. Pre-sessional courses use it as a component of reports and essays. Undergraduate in-sessional work addresses discipline-specific classification schemes and their limits.

guidance.summary: Trimble lists process description among the core functions of scientific and technical discourse, and Rose and Martin distinguish procedures (how to do something) from sequential explanations (how something happens), which maps onto the difference between a methods section and an explanation of a phenomenon. Teach with discipline-relevant diagrams and authentic methods paragraphs, and treat voice as a choice about agency rather than an automatic marker of science.

activities.title: Diagram to prose and back
learnerActions: Work in pairs: one learner has a process diagram, the other a blank template
Describe the process so your partner can complete the diagram
Swap roles with a different process and compare accuracy
activities.intendedInsight: Clear process description depends on sequencing, purpose and precise verbs.
activities.rationale: Trimble's discourse approach links process description to visual–verbal relationships typical of technical texts.

activities.title: Procedure, method or explanation?
learnerActions: Sort short texts into instructions, methods recounts and explanations of natural processes
Note the tense, voice and mood of each
Rewrite one text as another type
activities.intendedInsight: The same sequence of steps is expressed differently depending on whether it instructs, recounts or explains.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin's distinction between procedures and sequential explanations clarifies the genres in which process description appears.

difficulties.pattern: 'Then… then… after that… then…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Repetitive sequencing with one or two devices.
difficulties.response: Introduce time clauses (once, after X has been…), participle clauses and varied sequencers.

difficulties.pattern: Agentless passives where the agent matters, such as who conducted the interviews.
difficulties.revealedBy: Methods sections in which it is unclear who did what; feedback asking 'by whom?'.
difficulties.response: Discuss when agency matters for credibility and replicability, and show methods sections that use active voice. Do not replace this with 'avoid the passive'.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing purpose and result ('The sample was heated so it melts').
difficulties.revealedBy: Mismatch between purpose and result expressions; tense errors after so that.
difficulties.response: Contrast to + infinitive and in order to (purpose) with so and so that, using steps from the learner's field.

diagnostic.task: The learner describes a four-step diagram of a familiar process (for example making paper) in a short paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Describes the steps in order with varied sequencing, appropriate passives, at least one purpose expression and consistent present tense.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Describes the sequence correctly but with repetitive sequencing or inconsistent voice.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Omits steps, confuses order or cannot sustain the passive.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes emphasise process description in science and engineering content. Pre-sessional courses link it to methods sections and data commentary. Undergraduate in-sessional support targets laboratory reports and technical writing.

guidance.summary: Trimble's discourse approach to English for science and technology distinguishes physical, functional and process description, and Rose and Martin's compositional reports describe the parts of an entity. Mohan's knowledge framework links such description to graphic representation. Information-gap tasks in which a partner reconstructs a diagram from a description give learners immediate feedback on precision and suit foundation science and engineering cohorts in particular.

activities.title: Describe and draw
learnerActions: Describe a labelled diagram from your field to a partner who cannot see it
Your partner draws it from your description
Compare the drawing with the original and revise your description
activities.intendedInsight: Precise spatial and part–whole language is what allows a reader to reconstruct a structure.
activities.rationale: Physical description is a core EST function in Trimble's account; the information gap tests precision directly.

activities.title: Structure plus function
learnerActions: Make a table of an object's or organisation's components and the function of each
Turn the table into a paragraph that moves from whole to parts
Add function language for each component
activities.intendedInsight: Academic description often combines what something consists of with what each part does.
activities.rationale: Mohan's link between knowledge structures and graphic organisers, and Rose and Martin's compositional reports, support moving from table to text.

difficulties.pattern: 'The heart is consist from four chambers.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in the form and complementation of part–whole verbs.
difficulties.response: Teach consist of, comprise, contain and be made up of as patterns, with examples from the learner's field.

difficulties.pattern: Spatial prepositions mapped from another language (on the corner of the diagram, in the left).
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositional errors in spatial description; partners drawing components in the wrong place.
difficulties.response: Languages divide spatial relations differently, so teach spatial prepositions in chunks (at the top of, on the left, adjacent to) with diagrams.

difficulties.pattern: Describing parts in random order.
difficulties.revealedBy: Descriptions that jump between components with no spatial or hierarchical logic.
difficulties.response: Teach whole-to-part and spatial ordering strategies (top to bottom, outside to inside) and plan the order before writing.

diagnostic.task: The learner describes a simple labelled diagram of a familiar object (for example a bicycle) in four sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Moves from whole to parts, uses part–whole verbs and spatial prepositions accurately and states at least one function.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names parts accurately but with weak ordering or prepositional errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists parts without relations.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach structural description within science, engineering and business content. Pre-sessional courses use it in technical reports and for describing organisations. Undergraduate in-sessional support addresses discipline-specific descriptive writing, such as design reports and anatomy.

guidance.summary: Trimble treats comparison and contrast as a rhetorical technique that supports many functions in technical discourse. Carrell's study suggests that awareness of top-level structures, including comparison, supports L2 readers' recall, so comparison can be taught for reading as well as writing. The Academic Formulas List includes formulas for contrast and comparison, which gives a corpus-based starting point for phraseology. Emphasise criteria first, then organisation, then a concluding point.

activities.title: Criteria grid first
learnerActions: Build a grid of criteria for comparing two items before writing
Decide whether point-by-point or block organisation suits the purpose
Write the comparison and finish with a judgement based on the grid
activities.intendedInsight: Academic comparison is led by criteria and should lead to a point.
activities.rationale: Trimble's account of comparison as a rhetorical technique places it in the service of a larger function such as evaluation or recommendation.

activities.title: Comparison formula hunt
learnerActions: Find comparison formulas in texts from your field
Group them by meaning (similarity, difference, degree)
Choose three to use in your next comparison
activities.intendedInsight: Comparison relies on recurrent multi-word formulas, some of which signal degree.
activities.rationale: Simpson-Vlach and Ellis identify contrast and comparison formulas in academic speech and writing, providing a frequency-informed basis for selection.

difficulties.pattern: 'The GDP of China is higher than Japan.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons between non-equivalent items; missing 'that of' or 'those of'.
difficulties.response: Show the logic of comparing like with like and practise that of and those of.

difficulties.pattern: Listing similarities and differences without a conclusion.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons that end after the last difference; feedback asking 'so what?'.
difficulties.response: Require a final sentence that states what the comparison shows in relation to the task.

difficulties.pattern: 'On the other hand' used in every sentence of a comparison.
difficulties.revealedBy: One contrastive connector used repeatedly, sometimes for similarity.
difficulties.response: Teach a range of comparison resources, including within-sentence structures (whereas, unlike X, Y…).

diagnostic.task: The learner compares two study methods (for example interviews and questionnaires) in four sentences for a methods justification.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Compares on explicit criteria, uses accurate comparative structures and ends with a justified choice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Compares accurately but without criteria or a conclusion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes each method separately with no comparison.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes use comparison with data and subject content. Pre-sessional courses link it to compare-and-contrast essays and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work applies it to comparing theories, methods and findings.

guidance.summary: Halliday and Martin show that scientific English often realises causal relations within the clause, as verbs (leads to, causes) or nouns (the cause of), rather than between clauses with conjunctions. Schleppegrell describes this shift as a key feature of the language of schooling that learners need explicit help with. Teach the full range of realisations, and connect language to reasoning so that 'leads to' is not used for associations.

activities.title: Four ways to say because
learnerActions: Express one causal relation from your field as a conjunction, a preposition, a verb and a noun phrase
Compare the four versions for emphasis and formality
Decide which version best links to the previous sentence in a given paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Causation can be packaged in different grammatical forms, and academic writing often favours verbs and nouns.
activities.rationale: Halliday and Martin's account of grammatical metaphor shows how causal relations move into the clause in scientific discourse.

activities.title: Correlation or cause?
learnerActions: Read short descriptions of findings from different study designs
Decide whether each supports a causal or an associational claim
Write each claim with suitable verbs (causes, leads to, is associated with, is linked to)
activities.intendedInsight: The strength of causal language must follow the evidence.
activities.rationale: Schleppegrell's emphasis on making the linguistic demands of reasoning explicit supports connecting causal language to the reasoning behind it.

difficulties.pattern: 'Smoking results from cancer' or 'Due to prices rose, demand fell.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reversed result in/result from; due to used as a conjunction before a clause.
difficulties.response: Teach causal verbs and prepositions as patterns with direction arrows, using the learner's own sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Causal verbs for correlational findings ('Social media use leads to anxiety').
difficulties.revealedBy: Causal claims from surveys or correlations.
difficulties.response: Link causal verbs to design and practise associational alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: Relying only on because and so, producing chains of short clauses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Spoken-style causal chains in writing; few causal verbs or nouns.
difficulties.response: Show nominalised alternatives and practise combining clauses into causal noun-phrase structures where appropriate.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Because the temperature increased, the ice melted faster' in two other ways, one beginning with 'The increase'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces accurate verb and noun versions (The increase in temperature caused the ice to melt faster; The faster melting was due to…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces one accurate alternative with an error in the other.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot move beyond because and so.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach cause and effect with subject content and data. Pre-sessional courses connect it to explanation essays and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on calibrating causal claims in discussions of evidence.
reviewNotes: No source in the bibliography directly addresses learner difficulties with causal claim strength; the guidance draws on general research-literacy principles and could be supported by a proposed reference in a later revision.

guidance.summary: Trimble lists exemplification among the rhetorical techniques that support functions in technical texts, and Hyland treats exemplification as one form of code gloss, a reader-oriented elaboration whose frequency varies by discipline. Two teaching priorities follow: grammatical control of the main markers, and the argumentative judgement of which example is representative and how it links back to the claim.

activities.title: Representative or exceptional?
learnerActions: Read a general claim and four candidate examples
Decide which examples best represent the claim and which are exceptional
Write a sentence using the best example and linking it back to the claim
activities.intendedInsight: Good examples are typical of the claim, and their relevance should be stated.
activities.rationale: Trimble's treatment of exemplification as serving a larger rhetorical purpose highlights selection, not just markers.

activities.title: Marker grammar sort
learnerActions: Correct sentences that misuse for example, such as and e.g.
Classify the markers as sentence-level or phrase-level
Write one sentence of each type about your own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Exemplification markers differ in grammar: some introduce a sentence, others a noun phrase.
activities.rationale: Hyland's analysis of code glosses provides a functional frame; grammatical sorting addresses persistent form errors.

difficulties.pattern: 'Many countries such as China has increased spending' or 'such as the government should…'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Such as followed by a clause; agreement errors with the head noun.
difficulties.response: Show such as as part of a noun phrase and practise for example for sentence-level examples.

difficulties.pattern: An anecdote presented as proof of a general claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: A single personal example used as the main support for a broad claim.
difficulties.response: Distinguish illustration from evidence, and show how examples complement rather than replace evidence.

difficulties.pattern: Strings of examples with no link back to the point.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that list several examples and end without stating what they show.
difficulties.response: Require a linking sentence after each extended example (This illustrates…).

diagnostic.task: The learner supports the claim 'Some renewable energy sources are intermittent' with one example and explains how it supports the claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a representative example (for example solar power at night) with correct marker grammar and links it explicitly to intermittency.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives an appropriate example but does not link it back, or makes a marker error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Gives an irrelevant or unrepresentative example.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes focus on marker grammar and on selecting relevant examples. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work emphasises representativeness and the difference between illustration and evidence.
reviewNotes: hyland2007gloss is a proposed reference; the claims are also supported by hyland2005metadiscourse.

guidance.summary: Hoey's analyses show the situation–problem–response–evaluation pattern to be widespread across text types, signalled by recognisable lexis and often recursive. Swales and Feak's problem–process–solution texts provide graduate-level models. Teach the pattern with authentic texts from learners' fields and give particular attention to the evaluation element, which learners often omit.

activities.title: Pattern chain
learnerActions: Reorder jumbled sentences from a problem–solution text
Label each sentence as situation, problem, response or evaluation
Identify the words that helped you decide
activities.intendedInsight: Problem–solution texts follow a recognisable sequence signalled by specific vocabulary.
activities.rationale: Hoey's description of the pattern and its lexical signals makes the sequence teachable and recognisable.

activities.title: Evaluate the response
learnerActions: Choose criteria (effectiveness, cost, feasibility, side effects) for evaluating responses to a problem in your field
Write an evaluation sentence for each response
Where a response is evaluated negatively, propose a further response
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation completes the pattern and can lead to a new cycle.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak's problem–solution texts and Hoey's account of recursion both treat evaluation as integral to the pattern.

difficulties.pattern: Listing several solutions without saying whether they work.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs that end after describing responses; feedback asking for evaluation.
difficulties.response: Require one evaluation sentence for each response, using explicit criteria.

difficulties.pattern: Confusing the causes of a problem with its effects or symptoms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Responses that address symptoms rather than causes; mixed-up cause and consequence statements.
difficulties.response: Map causes and consequences visually before writing, then check that responses target causes where appropriate.

difficulties.pattern: Forcing every task into a problem–solution frame.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion or comparison tasks answered as problem–solution essays.
difficulties.response: Analyse task wording to select the relevant pattern; problem–solution is one pattern among several.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes four sentences on a familiar campus problem (for example a shortage of study space) using the full pattern.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Includes situation, problem, response and a criterion-based evaluation, with precise problem and response vocabulary.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Includes the elements but evaluates only vaguely (this is a good solution).
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the problem only, or lists solutions without structure.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach the pattern in short essays and business or engineering content. Pre-sessional courses apply it to problem–solution essays and case studies. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support connects it to case analyses, reports and research introductions.

guidance.summary: Rose and Martin distinguish sequential, causal, factorial and consequential explanations, a useful map of what explaining can involve. Nesi and Gardner identify explanation as a genre family across disciplines in UK student writing. Basturkmen's comparison of commenting on results found that published articles offered and evaluated alternative explanations more fully than master's dissertations, which suggests that weighing explanations deserves explicit teaching.

activities.title: Description to explanation
learnerActions: Take three descriptive sentences from your own draft
Add the mechanism or reason behind each
Compare the revised sentences with the originals and discuss what was added
activities.intendedInsight: Explanation answers 'how' and 'why', not just 'what'.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin's explanation genres show the stages explanation adds beyond description.

activities.title: Rival explanations
learnerActions: Generate at least two explanations for an unexpected result
Weigh them using evidence and plausibility
Write a short paragraph presenting and evaluating the alternatives
activities.intendedInsight: Considering alternative explanations strengthens the analysis.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen's finding that expert writers develop and evaluate alternative explanations more than novice writers supports this practice.

difficulties.pattern: 'My feedback says I am too descriptive, but I explained everything.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Detailed descriptions of what happened with little account of why; feedback asking for more analysis.
difficulties.response: Show explicit contrasts between description and explanation in the learner's own texts and practise adding mechanisms.

difficulties.pattern: 'The reason is because…'; chains of 'this is why'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Informal or redundant explanatory structures.
difficulties.response: Teach formal explanatory structures (The reason for X is that…; …, which explains why…).

difficulties.pattern: A single explanation presented as certain.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussion sections that offer one account of a result without considering others.
difficulties.response: Require at least one alternative explanation and a reason for preferring one.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains why a survey had a low response rate (data provided) in three sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives plausible mechanisms, considers more than one explanation and links each to the data.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Offers a single plausible explanation without weighing alternatives.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the low response rate without explaining it.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach explanation through science and social science content. Pre-sessional courses link it to explanation essays and data commentary. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on explanation genres and on explaining results.

guidance.summary: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans identify hypothesis among the moves of discussion sections, alongside explanation and deduction, and Hyland's work on hedging shows how speculation about results is carefully modalised. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman provide a teachable account of conditional meanings. Teach prediction and hypothesis through research questions and data from learners' own fields, contrasting 'will' (confident prediction), 'would' (hypothetical) and 'is likely to' (probabilistic).

activities.title: From question to testable hypothesis
learnerActions: Take a research question from your field
Write a hypothesis that names the variables and the expected relation
Ask a partner what result would count against it, and revise if they cannot say
activities.intendedInsight: A hypothesis must predict something that could turn out to be wrong.
activities.rationale: Linking form (conditionals, modals) to the logic of testing makes hypothesis language purposeful; the conditional forms follow the account in Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman.

activities.title: Speculation in discussions
learnerActions: Find the sentences in discussion sections where writers speculate about causes or implications
Note the modal and hedging devices used
Write one speculative sentence about a finding from your own reading
activities.intendedInsight: Expert speculation is explicitly marked as tentative.
activities.rationale: Hopkins and Dudley-Evans identify hypothesis moves in discussions, and Hyland shows how such claims are hedged.

difficulties.pattern: 'If the temperature will increase, the reaction will speed up.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'will' in the if-clause of real conditionals; tense errors in unreal conditionals.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages mark future or hypothetical meaning in both clauses benefit from contrasting the English pattern explicitly, using predictions from their own field.

difficulties.pattern: 'This study will prove that…' or a hypothesis that merely restates the research question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypotheses that are untestable or framed as certainties.
difficulties.response: Distinguish questions, hypotheses and predictions, and discuss testability.

difficulties.pattern: 'Would' used for confident predictions ('The results would show a clear increase').
difficulties.revealedBy: Hypothetical 'would' where 'will' or 'is expected to' is meant, making predictions sound unreal.
difficulties.response: Contrast will, would and is likely to in pairs of sentences.

diagnostic.task: The learner turns 'Does sleep affect exam performance?' into a hypothesis and a prediction.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes a testable hypothesis naming variables and direction, and a correctly formed conditional prediction.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes a hypothesis without a clear direction or with a conditional error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the question or makes a certain claim.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach prediction with simple data and science content. Pre-sessional and in-sessional courses link it to research proposals and discussions. Doctoral writers apply it to hypotheses, research questions and implications in theses and articles.

guidance.summary: Recommendations are central to the case study and proposal genre families described by Nesi and Gardner and to the conclusion sections of research articles, where Yang and Allison identify recommendations for further research as a regular move. Moore and Morton found that IELTS writing tasks elicit statements about what ought to be done more than university assignments do, which may encourage sweeping recommendations unsupported by analysis. Teach recommending as the end point of analysis rather than an expression of opinion.

activities.title: Finding-to-recommendation chain
learnerActions: List the key findings of a case or report
Write a recommendation that follows from each finding, naming who should act and how
Rank the recommendations by strength of evidence and feasibility
activities.intendedInsight: Recommendations should be traceable to findings and prioritised.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's genre families show recommendations embedded in case studies and proposals, where they must follow from analysis.

activities.title: Directness for the reader
learnerActions: Rewrite one recommendation for a client report, a policy brief and a research article's implications section
Compare how directness and the named actor change
activities.intendedInsight: The form of a recommendation depends on the reader's role and the genre.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison's analysis of research article conclusions shows recommendations framed for researchers, which contrasts with practice-oriented genres.

difficulties.pattern: 'Governments should ban all cars' with no supporting analysis.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sweeping, unsupported recommendations, especially in essays influenced by test preparation.
difficulties.response: Show how recommendations follow from analysis; ask the learner to trace each recommendation back to evidence.

difficulties.pattern: 'It is recommended that the company changes / to change its policy.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors in mandative structures.
difficulties.response: Teach the mandative subjunctive and the should-alternative as patterns, noting variation in British usage.

difficulties.pattern: 'More research is needed.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Vague recommendations that specify no actor, action or focus.
difficulties.response: Require recommendations to state who, what and why, and model specific future-research recommendations.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes two recommendations based on a finding that students rarely use the library's online chat service.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Writes specific recommendations naming actors and actions, linked to the finding and accurately formed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Writes relevant recommendations that are vague or contain a mandative error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Writes general opinions unrelated to the finding.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach recommendation language in business and engineering contexts. Pre-sessional courses focus on reports and problem–solution essays. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support addresses case studies, business reports and dissertation conclusions.
reviewNotes: British usage often accepts should + infinitive or an indicative verb after mandative expressions as alternatives to the subjunctive; teachers should present the options rather than a single correct form.

guidance.summary: Yang and Allison's analysis of research articles separates summarising the study, evaluating it and drawing deductions in concluding sections, a useful way to show learners that concluding is more than restating. In Hyland's model, stage labels such as 'in sum' are frame markers whose use should be proportionate to the text's length. Teach synthesis-based conclusions at paragraph and section level, linked to hedged inference.

activities.title: List or synthesis?
learnerActions: Compare two conclusions to the same set of findings: one that lists them and one that synthesises them
Identify the language that achieves synthesis (taken together, these findings, overall pattern)
Rewrite a listing conclusion of your own as a synthesis
activities.intendedInsight: A conclusion should say what the findings add up to, not repeat them.
activities.rationale: Yang and Allison's distinction between summarising and deducing in concluding moves shows the step from restatement to inference.

activities.title: Taken together
learnerActions: Encapsulate three related findings in one noun phrase (These three findings…)
Add an inference with an appropriate hedge
Compare the strength of inferences across the group
activities.intendedInsight: Encapsulation plus calibrated inference is a compact concluding pattern.
activities.rationale: Hyland's treatment of frame markers and stance resources supports teaching the concluding move as a combination of organisation and stance.

difficulties.pattern: 'In conclusion,' followed by a restatement of the introduction.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conclusions that repeat the introduction or the paragraph topics without synthesis or implication.
difficulties.response: Show conclusions that synthesise and draw implications; ask what the reader now knows that they did not know at the start.

difficulties.pattern: 'To sum up' at the end of every paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent summative markers in short texts.
