difficulties.response: Reserve summative markers for section and text endings, and use concluding sentences without markers elsewhere.

difficulties.pattern: Conclusions that over-claim or introduce new evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Stronger claims in the conclusion than in the body; new sources or data introduced at the end.
difficulties.response: Check conclusions against the body and calibrate inferences to what has been shown.

diagnostic.task: The learner writes a two-sentence conclusion to three short paragraphs showing that a programme improved attendance, grades and satisfaction.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Synthesises (the programme had consistently positive effects across measures) and draws a hedged inference about its value.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Synthesises partially or draws an unhedged inference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists the three findings again.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach concluding sentences and short conclusions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses address essay and report conclusions. Taught postgraduate writers apply the function to dissertation chapters and discussion sections.

guidance.summary: Rose and Martin trace a progression from recounts to historical accounts and explanations, in which time shifts from simply ordering events to organising an argument through periodisation and causal accounts. Nesi and Gardner identify narrative recounts and methodology recounts among university genre families. Teach chronology as both a resource and a risk: learners need control of time expressions and tense, but they also need to move from recount to interpretation.

activities.title: Timeline to account
learnerActions: Group events on a timeline into phases and label each phase
Write a paragraph that moves through the phases using time expressions and tense shifts
State the basis of your periodisation in one sentence
activities.intendedInsight: Periodisation turns a list of events into an interpretive account.
activities.rationale: Rose and Martin show how historical genres use time to build an argument rather than a simple sequence.

activities.title: Recount to account
learnerActions: Take a narrative paragraph (for example a case history or methodology recount)
Add a sentence after each phase that interprets its significance
Compare the effect on the reader
activities.intendedInsight: Academic narration usually needs interpretation as well as sequence.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's genre families show that recount genres in university writing serve purposes beyond narrating events.

difficulties.pattern: 'In 1990 the theory has been developed by…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Present perfect with specific past time expressions; past simple for developments continuing to the present.
difficulties.response: Learners whose other languages do not distinguish perfect aspect in the same way benefit from timeline-based contrasts of past simple and present perfect.

difficulties.pattern: Narrating events when analysis was required.
difficulties.revealedBy: History or case essays that tell what happened without explaining why it matters; feedback asking for analysis.
difficulties.response: Practise adding interpretive sentences and organising by theme or argument where the task requires it.

difficulties.pattern: 'Then… after that… then…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Monotonous sequencing with a small set of time words.
difficulties.response: Introduce time clauses and periodising expressions (By the late 1990s, Over the following decade).

diagnostic.task: The learner writes a four-sentence account of the development of a technology or idea in their field from a given timeline.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses varied time expressions, correct tense and aspect, groups events into phases and ends with a comment on significance.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Sequences accurately but with tense errors or no interpretation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Lists dates and events with errors in sequence or tense.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes teach narration with history, business and science content. Pre-sessional courses link it to methodology recounts and case histories. Undergraduate in-sessional support targets history, law and health case writing, where moving from narration to analysis is a frequent issue.

guidance.summary: Mohan's knowledge framework places evaluation alongside classification and principles as a knowledge structure with characteristic language. Nesi and Gardner's critique genre family shows evaluation as an assessed purpose in its own right across disciplines, and Hunston and Thompson treat evaluation as pervasive in academic discourse rather than confined to explicitly evaluative genres. Teach criteria first, then language, then weighing.

activities.title: Criteria before judgement
learnerActions: Agree in groups on criteria for evaluating a policy, method or text
Rate the item against each criterion
Write an evaluation that weighs the ratings to reach an overall judgement
activities.intendedInsight: Evaluation is more convincing when its criteria are explicit.
activities.rationale: Mohan's framework treats evaluation as a knowledge structure that can be taught through explicit criteria and graphic organisers.

activities.title: Description or evaluation?
learnerActions: Highlight descriptive and evaluative sentences in a sample critique
Convert three descriptive sentences into evaluations
Check your own draft for the balance between the two
activities.intendedInsight: Many 'descriptive' texts can be improved by adding judgement of value or significance.
activities.rationale: Nesi and Gardner's critique genre family provides authentic models of evaluative writing across disciplines.

difficulties.pattern: 'I described the study in detail, so I have evaluated it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Critiques and reviews that summarise without judging; feedback asking for critical evaluation.
difficulties.response: Make the description–evaluation distinction explicit using the learner's own text and practise adding judgements.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study is good and interesting.'
difficulties.revealedBy: General evaluative words without criteria or precision.
difficulties.response: Build a bank of evaluative lexis by criterion (robust, representative, limited, compelling) from reading in the field.

difficulties.pattern: 'Evaluating means finding what is wrong' or 'it is just my opinion'.
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided criticism, or evaluation presented as personal preference.
difficulties.response: Present evaluation as balanced, criterion-based judgement that recognises strengths as well as weaknesses.

diagnostic.task: The learner evaluates a short description of an online survey of 50 volunteers in two sentences.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Names a criterion (for example representativeness), states a strength and a weakness and gives an overall judgement in precise language.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies a weakness but without criteria or balance.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Describes the survey without judging it.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation programmes introduce evaluation with simple criteria and familiar topics. Pre-sessional courses link it to critiques and discussion essays. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional support applies evaluation to sources, methods and theories in the discipline.

guidance.summary: Hyland's interpersonal model of metadiscourse, refined in Hyland and Tse, is the most widely used pedagogical framework, although its boundaries (for example whether transitions are propositional or metadiscursive) are debated, so present it as a heuristic. Teach the concept after learners have met concrete resources such as signposting and hedging, so that it organises what they already know. Cross-disciplinary comparison then shows that metadiscourse norms belong to communities rather than to 'good writing' in general.

activities.title: Two-colour metadiscourse highlight
learnerActions: Highlight interactive metadiscourse in one colour and interactional metadiscourse in another in a published discussion section
Read a version of the same text with all metadiscourse removed
Discuss what the reader loses in the stripped version
activities.intendedInsight: Metadiscourse does not add propositional content but shapes how readers process and evaluate it.
activities.rationale: Hyland's model is designed to show writing as interaction; comparing texts with and without metadiscourse makes that interaction tangible.

activities.title: Discipline comparison
learnerActions: Count the metadiscourse categories in two short extracts from contrasting disciplines
Hypothesise why the patterns differ
Check your hypotheses against a third extract from your own field
activities.intendedInsight: Metadiscourse use reflects disciplinary values about argument, evidence and the reader.
activities.rationale: Hyland and Tse document disciplinary variation in metadiscourse in postgraduate writing, supporting discipline-aware teaching.

difficulties.pattern: Treating metadiscourse as a fixed list of words that always have the same function.
difficulties.revealedBy: Classifying 'clearly' as a booster in 'the results are clearly presented', or 'however' as metadiscourse wherever it appears.
difficulties.response: Insist on functional analysis in context; discuss borderline cases openly as part of the model's acknowledged fuzziness.

difficulties.pattern: After learning the concept, adding metadiscourse everywhere to appear reader-friendly.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dense signposting and reader address in short texts; feedback that the writing 'talks about itself'.
difficulties.response: Return to genre and length: compare metadiscourse density in exemplars of the target genre.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains, with examples from a provided text, what metadiscourse is and why a writer would use it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Defines metadiscourse as language that organises the text or expresses the writer's stance towards content and reader, gives correctly classified examples of both kinds and links them to reader needs.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives correct examples of one kind (usually signposting) but does not recognise stance devices as metadiscourse.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Equates metadiscourse with linking words or cannot give examples.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses, introduce the concept as a way of drawing together signposting and hedging. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work can use it for disciplinary text analysis. Doctoral writers benefit from the full model when analysing target journals.
reviewNotes: Alternative, narrower reflexive models of metadiscourse exist; none is in the current bibliography, so the guidance presents Hyland's model as one influential heuristic rather than the only account.

guidance.summary: Hyland's study of hedging in science research articles distinguishes hedges that concern the accuracy of claims from those that concern the writer's relationship with readers, and Salager-Meyer's taxonomy (shields, approximators, expressions of doubt, compound hedges) gives a practical classification. Hyland and Milton found that L2 student writers in their study used a narrower range of devices and expressed certainty more strongly than L1 peers, which suggests prioritising range and placement over introducing 'may'. Teach hedges together with the evidence they respond to, not as politeness formulae.

activities.title: Hedge the claim to the evidence
learnerActions: Read short study summaries that specify design and sample
Write one claim for each, hedged to match the evidence
Compare with a partner and justify any difference in hedge choice
activities.intendedInsight: Hedges express the writer's judgement of evidence, not general politeness.
activities.rationale: Hyland's account links hedging in research writing to the epistemic status of claims; tying each hedge to evidence reflects that function.

activities.title: Section map of hedging
learnerActions: Mark all hedges in a research article from your field
Count them by section (introduction, methods, results, discussion)
Explain the distribution you find
activities.intendedInsight: Hedging clusters where writers interpret and generalise, and is sparse where they describe procedures.
activities.rationale: Salager-Meyer reported that hedging in medical articles varied across rhetorical sections, which learners can test in their own field.

difficulties.pattern: 'Hedging makes me sound unsure; strong statements show confidence.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Unhedged generalisations and interpretations presented as facts; resistance to feedback asking for qualification.
difficulties.response: Show expert texts in the learner's field in which hedging accompanies authoritative claims, and frame hedging as precision and as an expected part of academic argument.

difficulties.pattern: 'It may possibly be suggested that this could perhaps indicate…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Multiple hedges stacked on single claims after instruction; feedback that the argument is unclear.
difficulties.response: Teach one hedge per source of uncertainty and ask the learner to state what exactly is uncertain. Do not react by discouraging hedging altogether.

difficulties.pattern: 'This can be the reason for the decline.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Can' used for epistemic possibility where 'could' or 'may' is expected.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages use one modal for both ability and possibility need to see that 'can' expresses general possibility (This can be problematic) but not, in positive statements, an inference about a specific case, where 'may', 'might' or 'could' is used (This could be the reason).

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Social media causes depression in teenagers' as a claim based on one cross-sectional survey of 200 students.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a claim that is hedged for causation and scoped to the sample (for example 'use of social media was associated with higher depression scores among the students surveyed'), and explains both changes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds a modal ('may cause') but leaves the causal claim and the scope unchanged.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the claim unchanged or adds an intensifier.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need a core set of devices beyond modals and the habit of qualifying generalisations. Pre-sessional and in-sessional courses should connect hedging to evidence and to discipline. Doctoral writers work on reader-oriented hedging and on balancing tentativeness with the need to claim contribution.
reviewNotes: hylandmilton1997 is a proposed reference; the claim about L2 students' narrower range is attributed to it alone and should be removed or re-sourced if the reference is not verified.

guidance.summary: Hyland treats boosters as the counterpart of hedges in projecting commitment and solidarity. Learner-corpus research collected in Granger (1998), including work on adjective intensification, together with Hyland and Milton's comparison of L1 and L2 student writing, points to overstatement and speech-like intensification as common learner patterns, while Aull and Lancaster report differences in stance markers between first-year and more advanced writers. Teach boosters with hedges as a single certainty continuum, and treat intensifiers as a register issue.

activities.title: Certainty cline
learnerActions: Arrange verbs and adverbs (suggest, indicate, show, demonstrate, prove; possibly, probably, clearly, undoubtedly) on a cline of certainty
Check a few disputed items in concordance lines from an academic corpus
Decide which items are appropriate for empirical findings in your field
activities.intendedInsight: Certainty is graded, and some strong items (prove) are rarely appropriate for empirical claims.
activities.rationale: Hyland's stance model positions boosters and hedges on one dimension of commitment; a cline makes that dimension visible.

activities.title: Justify your certainty
learnerActions: Annotate every booster in your draft with the evidence that justifies it
Remove or replace any booster for which you cannot state evidence
Keep boosters where evidence is strong and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Boosters are earned by evidence and should be used deliberately.
activities.rationale: Developmental differences in stance marking reported by Aull and Lancaster suggest that conscious attention to certainty markers is worthwhile for novice academic writers.

difficulties.pattern: 'The experiment proves that the treatment works.'
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Prove' and 'demonstrate' used for single empirical studies or correlational findings.
difficulties.response: Contrast the near-synonymous verbs by strength and connect them to the evidence each implies.

difficulties.pattern: 'This is a very, very important issue that is extremely relevant.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Frequent general intensifiers (very, really, extremely, totally) in written assignments.
difficulties.response: Replace intensifiers with precise statements of degree or significance and with evidence; treat this as register development.

difficulties.pattern: After hedging instruction, removing every booster so that the main claim lacks commitment.
difficulties.revealedBy: Central arguments and well-established facts heavily hedged.
difficulties.response: Show that expert writers commit firmly to well-supported and central claims; practise deciding where to boost.

diagnostic.task: The learner sorts six sentences into 'certainty justified' and 'certainty not justified' given brief evidence descriptions, then revises one.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Sorts accurately, retains boosters for robust or well-established findings and downgrades others with precise alternatives.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies overstatement but downgrades every booster, including justified ones.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Treats all boosters as acceptable or cannot link certainty to evidence.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on intensifiers and on the difference between show and prove. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses link boosters to evidence. Taught postgraduate writers work on committing firmly to their own findings where warranted.
reviewNotes: The attribution of adjective-intensification findings to the Granger (1998) collection refers to a chapter on overstatement in advanced learner writing; the chapter author should be named if the collection is cited in teacher materials.

guidance.summary: Toulmin's qualifier makes explicit that claim strength is part of argument structure, and Hyland shows how hedges in research articles respond to the epistemic status of claims. Swales and Feak's graduate-level material on qualification and strength of claim offers practical exercises. Teach calibration from the evidence outward: first decide what the design and data license, then choose wording; avoid fixed 'hedging quotas'.

activities.title: Evidence-to-claim ladder
learnerActions: Place candidate claims about a finding on a ladder from weakest to strongest
Decide which rung the evidence supports and write the claim
State what further evidence would justify the next rung
activities.intendedInsight: Each level of claim strength corresponds to a level of evidence.
activities.rationale: Toulmin's model treats the qualifier as tied to the grounds of an argument; the ladder operationalises that link.

activities.title: Calibration-only peer review
learnerActions: Review a peer's draft for claim strength only
Mark each miscalibrated claim as over-claimed or over-hedged and note the evidence issue
Discuss disagreements about the marks
activities.intendedInsight: Calibration judgements can be argued and refined with reference to evidence.
activities.rationale: Focused peer review isolates one feature so that attention is not diluted; Hyland's account of hedging as negotiated with readers supports discussing such judgements.

difficulties.pattern: 'The data show a correlation, so X causes Y.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Causal language for correlational findings; general claims from one sample.
difficulties.response: Return to what different designs can and cannot establish before working on wording.

difficulties.pattern: Hedging every claim to the same degree regardless of evidence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform 'may' or 'it seems that' across strong and weak findings.
difficulties.response: Ask the learner to rank their claims by strength of evidence and to make the language reflect the ranking.

difficulties.pattern: Under-claiming one's own findings for fear of appearing arrogant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Doctoral or master's writing that presents clear results as barely suggestive; supervisors asking 'what is your contribution?'.
difficulties.response: Discuss expectations of contribution in the field; practise firm but bounded statements of what the study shows.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a summary of a randomised trial and of a single interview study on related topics and writes one claim based on each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Calibrates differently: firmer causal language for the trial (still scoped), exploratory and context-bound language for the interview study, with reasons.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Hedges both claims but to the same degree.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Makes unqualified or general claims from both.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce calibration with short summaries and data. Undergraduate in-sessional work links it to discussion of sources. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers apply it to their own findings and to claiming contribution, where both over- and under-claiming are risks.

guidance.summary: Hyland treats attitude markers as one stance resource, and Martin and White's attitude system (affect, judgement, appreciation) offers a finer lens for analysing what is being evaluated. Hunston and Thompson's collection frames evaluation as both expressing opinion and organising discourse, for example by marking what matters most. Teach that evaluation is expected in academic writing but must be anchored in evidence and expressed with disciplinary lexis; the aim is purposeful evaluation, not removal of the writer's view.

activities.title: Appraisal sort
learnerActions: Collect evaluative expressions from a book review and a discussion section
Sort them into affect (feelings), judgement (people's behaviour) and appreciation (things, ideas, texts)
Discuss which category dominates and why
activities.intendedInsight: Academic evaluation mostly appraises ideas, evidence and texts rather than expressing personal feeling.
activities.rationale: Martin and White's attitude categories give learners a principled way to see what kind of evaluation academic genres favour.

activities.title: Signalling significance
learnerActions: Revise a results or discussion paragraph you have written so that one attitude marker identifies the most important finding
Ask a partner to identify the key finding without being told
Adjust the marker if the partner chose a different finding
activities.intendedInsight: A well-placed attitude marker guides readers to what the writer considers significant.
activities.rationale: Hyland's stance model emphasises evaluation as a means of guiding readers' interpretation.

difficulties.pattern: 'I must never show my opinion in academic writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Purely descriptive results and literature summaries; feedback asking for more evaluation or significance.
difficulties.response: Show attitude markers in expert texts from the learner's field and distinguish evidence-based evaluation from unsupported opinion.

difficulties.pattern: 'The results were shocking and amazing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Emotive or conversational affect in written assignments.
difficulties.response: Replace affect with appreciation tied to evidence (an unexpected finding, a notably large effect).

difficulties.pattern: 'Interesting' and 'important' used for every evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated general evaluative adjectives that do not tell the reader why something matters.
difficulties.response: Ask 'interesting or important in what way?' and build a bank of more precise evaluative lexis from reading.

diagnostic.task: The learner evaluates a finding described in two sentences, in one sentence suitable for a discussion section.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses precise evaluative lexis anchored in the data (a notably larger effect than previously reported) and makes the significance explicit.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Evaluates with general adjectives (important, interesting) without saying why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the finding without evaluation, or uses emotive language.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses can link attitude markers to moving beyond description. In undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work, the focus is evaluating sources and results in the discipline. Doctoral writers attend to how evaluation positions their work relative to others.

guidance.summary: Tang and John's typology of first-person roles shows that 'I' ranges from the low-risk guide or architect to the high-risk opinion-holder and originator. Hyland found self-mention more frequent in humanities and social science research articles than in science and engineering, and found that undergraduate writers in his study tended to avoid authoritative uses of 'I'. Hyland and Jiang's diachronic study suggests that some informal features, including first-person pronouns, have increased in certain fields. Teach with discipline-specific evidence and explicitly challenge 'never use I' as an absolute rule.

activities.title: Role spotting
learnerActions: Find every first-person pronoun in extracts from two disciplines
Classify each by Tang and John's roles
Compare which roles each discipline uses and which are absent
activities.intendedInsight: Disciplines differ not only in how often writers use 'I' but in which authorial roles they allow it to perform.
activities.rationale: Combining Tang and John's typology with Hyland's evidence of disciplinary variation makes the choice evidence-based.

activities.title: Who is responsible?
learnerActions: Rewrite three impersonal sentences from your draft using self-mention and three first-person sentences impersonally
Discuss how responsibility for each claim changes
Decide which version suits your discipline and genre
activities.intendedInsight: Self-mention makes the writer accountable for a claim; impersonal forms shift attention to processes or data.
activities.rationale: Hyland's work on authorial identity shows that student writers often avoid authoritative self-representation; explicit comparison makes the trade-off visible.

difficulties.pattern: 'I was told never to use I in academic writing.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Convoluted agentless passives and 'the author' or 'the researcher' for the writer, even in reflective genres where 'I' is expected.
difficulties.response: Present field evidence and genre expectations; distinguish module guidance (which should be followed) from a universal rule.

difficulties.pattern: After learning that 'I' is acceptable, overusing 'I think' and 'I will talk about'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion-holder 'I think' on most claims; procedural 'I' announcing each paragraph.
difficulties.response: Show that expert self-mention is concentrated in particular roles and moves, such as stating contribution or methodological choice.

difficulties.pattern: 'As a student, I have no right to say I argue.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of the originator role even when the writer is making an original argument; hedged and depersonalised contributions.
difficulties.response: Discuss authorial roles as part of developing academic identity; legitimate the student's right to argue while keeping claims calibrated.

diagnostic.task: The learner states whether 'In this study we argue that…' would be acceptable in a dissertation in their field, and explains why.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Gives a field-specific answer based on observed practice, distinguishes 'we' for single authors, and notes genre and supervisor expectations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Gives a general answer (yes/no) without reference to field or genre.
diagnostic.gapResponse: States an absolute rule ('never use I or we').

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses address myths and introduce the role typology. Undergraduate in-sessional support connects self-mention to module guidance and reflective genres. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers need discipline-specific evidence, especially for stating contribution and methodological decisions in theses and articles.

guidance.summary: Hyland's stance-and-engagement model identifies reader pronouns, directives, questions, appeals to shared knowledge and personal asides as ways writers acknowledge and position readers, with distributions varying across disciplines. His study of addressee features in research articles develops this account, and Chang and Swales discuss informal elements such as direct questions and imperatives as both risks and opportunities for advanced L2 writers. Teach engagement as calibrated to readership through comparative genre analysis rather than through rules. Note that Hyland's 'engagement' (reader-oriented features) differs from 'engagement' in Martin and White's appraisal framework (dialogic positioning; see sta.dialogic-positioning).

activities.title: Textbook versus article
learnerActions: Find all engagement markers in a textbook introduction and a research article introduction on related topics
Classify them and compare their density
Explain the differences in terms of the intended reader
activities.intendedInsight: Engagement density and type depend on who the reader is and what the writer assumes they know.
activities.rationale: Hyland's model links engagement to writers' projections of readers, which genre comparison makes visible.

activities.title: Question or claim?
learnerActions: Find the questions in your own draft
For each, decide whether it frames a genuine problem or replaces a claim you should state
Rewrite those that replace claims
activities.intendedInsight: Questions can frame inquiry but cannot substitute for the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Chang and Swales present informal elements such as questions as features advanced writers can use deliberately rather than avoid or overuse.

difficulties.pattern: 'Have you ever wondered why…?' as an essay opening.
difficulties.revealedBy: Rhetorical questions addressed to a general reader at the start of essays and paragraphs.
difficulties.response: Show research article and essay openings in the field; reserve questions for framing a genuine problem or research focus.

difficulties.pattern: 'As we all know, obviously…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Appeals to shared knowledge for contested or specialised claims.
difficulties.response: Ask whether the intended reader genuinely shares the knowledge; if not, provide evidence instead.

difficulties.pattern: Mixing author 'we' and reader-inclusive 'we' in the same paragraph.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguity about whether 'we found' and 'we can see' refer to the same people.
difficulties.response: Make the distinction explicit and check each instance in the learner's draft.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Everybody knows that exercise is good. So why don't people do it?' as the opening of a public health essay.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Replaces the appeal to shared knowledge with evidence and turns the question into a framed problem (Despite well-documented benefits, participation remains low, raising the question of…).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Removes informality but loses the problem framing, or keeps an unsupported appeal.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the opening unchanged or only changes vocabulary.

guidance.contextNotes: Undergraduate in-sessional support targets questions and shared-knowledge appeals in essays. Taught postgraduate writers work on directives and reader reference in reports and dissertations. Doctoral writers attend to how engagement varies in their target journals and in public-facing writing.
reviewNotes: hyland2001reader is a proposed reference; the engagement account is also supported by hyland2005stance.

guidance.summary: Salager-Meyer's approximators of degree, quantity, frequency and time, and the content-oriented hedges Hyland describes, cover much of this territory. It is singled out because overgeneralisation is among the most frequent comments on early academic writing and because the remedy is often precise scope rather than modality. Hinkel provides practical exercises on hedging and qualification; teach quantifiers, tendency verbs and scope limiters as a set, linked to the evidence behind each claim.

activities.title: Sweeping to bounded
learnerActions: Rewrite sweeping statements from typical essay openings as bounded claims
Label what you changed: quantity, frequency, degree or context
Check which rewrites need a source to support them
activities.intendedInsight: Bounding a claim usually means specifying who, how many, how often or where, not just adding 'may'.
activities.rationale: Hinkel's techniques for teaching hedging in L2 writing support explicit, form-focused practice with these resources.

activities.title: Scope sorting
learnerActions: Find qualified generalisations in published texts from your field
Sort them by type of qualification
Choose two patterns to use in your next draft
activities.intendedInsight: Expert writers qualify generalisations in several distinct ways.
activities.rationale: Salager-Meyer's taxonomy distinguishes approximators of quantity, frequency, degree and time, providing a ready classification for analysis.

difficulties.pattern: 'Since the dawn of time, humans have always…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Dramatic, unbounded openings modelled on school or test-preparation essays.
difficulties.response: Show discipline-appropriate openings that begin with a bounded claim or specific context; explain why markers penalise unsupported sweep.

difficulties.pattern: 'Most of people tend to using…'
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors with quantifier + of, tend to + infinitive, and the majority of + verb agreement.
difficulties.response: Focused form practice on the grammar of quantifiers and tendency verbs, using the learner's own sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Qualifying even uncontroversial facts after instruction.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'In most cases, water tends to boil at 100°C at sea level.'
difficulties.response: Distinguish established facts and definitions from empirical generalisations, and qualify only the latter.

diagnostic.task: The learner rewrites 'Students today cannot concentrate because of smartphones' as a defensible claim.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Bounds the population and the claim (many undergraduate students report…; heavy smartphone use has been associated with…) and avoids an unsupported causal claim.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds 'may' or 'some' but keeps the causal claim or the unbounded population.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Leaves the claim unchanged or intensifies it.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, this is a priority for essay openings and topic sentences. Pre-sessional courses link it to evidence and sources. Undergraduate in-sessional support focuses on generalisations in students' own assignments.

guidance.summary: The distinction between averred and attributed propositions, introduced by Sinclair and developed by Hunston in Hunston and Thompson's collection, underpins both critical reading and transparent source use: readers assume unattributed statements are the writer's own. Thompson and Ye show how the choice of reporting verb signals whether the writer accepts an attributed proposition, and Hyland documents how disciplines differ in attribution practices. Teach the concept explicitly before reporting-verb lists, using colour-coding of authentic and student texts.

activities.title: Whose voice?
learnerActions: Colour-code each clause of a literature-review paragraph as averred or attributed
Underline the words that signal each attribution
Mark any clause where you cannot tell, and discuss how the writer could make it clear
activities.intendedInsight: Attribution must be signalled; anything unsignalled is read as the writer's own claim.
activities.rationale: Making the averral–attribution distinction visible addresses a source of both weak argument and unintentional misattribution.

activities.title: Endorse, neutral or distance?
learnerActions: Read the same proposition framed with shows, argues, claims, according to and as X notes
Rate how far the writer appears to accept the proposition in each version
Choose the framing that matches your own stance towards a source you are using
activities.intendedInsight: Attribution frames carry the writer's stance towards the attributed claim.
activities.rationale: Thompson and Ye's analysis of evaluation in reporting verbs shows how such choices encode writer stance.

difficulties.pattern: 'One citation at the end of the paragraph covers everything in it.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs mixing source content and the writer's comment with a single citation at the end; markers unable to tell which ideas are the student's.
difficulties.response: Show how readers interpret unsignalled sentences, and practise re-signalling attribution (The authors further note…) and marking the writer's comment (This suggests…).

difficulties.pattern: Presenting source content as general fact because the source is an authority.
difficulties.revealedBy: Claims from a single study stated as facts without attribution; textbook-style prose in literature reviews.
difficulties.response: Distinguish established knowledge from claims made by particular studies; ask 'who says so, and on what basis?'.

difficulties.pattern: Losing track of which source a claim belongs to in multi-source sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reporting clauses whose complement mixes the views of two sources, or a that-clause that runs on into the writer's comment.
difficulties.response: Practise one source per reporting clause and a clear end to each attributed that-clause before adding comment.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads: 'Smith (2019) found that bilingual children outperformed monolinguals on attention tasks. This advantage disappears in adulthood.' and says who is responsible for the second sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the second sentence reads as the writer's own claim and that, if it comes from Smith or another source, attribution is needed.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Assumes it is Smith's claim but cannot explain why a reader might think otherwise.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not see any ambiguity.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses should introduce the distinction early in source-based writing. Undergraduate in-sessional work links it to integrity and to marker feedback on unclear sources. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers apply it to literature reviews and to positioning their own studies.

guidance.summary: Biber et al. describe concessive subordinators and concessive and contrastive linking adverbials and their distribution across registers. In Martin and White's engagement system, concession forms part of a counter move that acknowledges and then supplants an expectation. Lancaster's analysis of upper-level student writing associates acknowledging-and-countering patterns with higher-graded work. Teach the grammar together with its argumentative function, and assess whether concessions are followed through.

activities.title: Objection–response chains
learnerActions: One partner writes the strongest objection to the other's thesis
The other writes a concessive response that acknowledges and then limits the objection
Swap roles and compare the strength of the responses
activities.intendedInsight: A good concession states the objection fairly and then shows precisely how far it limits the claim.
activities.rationale: Lancaster's findings on valued stance patterns suggest that concede-and-counter moves are worth explicit practice.

activities.title: Concession or contrast?
learnerActions: Sort sentences into contrast (comparing two items) and concession (acknowledging a point and then limiting it)
Rewrite two contrast sentences as concessions and note the change in argument
activities.intendedInsight: Concession is an argumentative move, not just a contrastive link.
activities.rationale: Combining the grammatical description in Biber et al. with the counter category in Martin and White links form to function.

difficulties.pattern: 'Although the policy is costly, but it is effective.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Double marking of concession across both clauses.
difficulties.response: Writers whose other languages pair concessive markers across clauses need to see that English marks one clause only; practise both English options with the same content.

difficulties.pattern: 'If I mention the other side, my argument will look weak.'
difficulties.revealedBy: One-sided essays with no acknowledgement of counter-arguments; feedback asking for consideration of alternative views.
difficulties.response: Show high-rated exemplars that concede and counter, and discuss how acknowledging objections builds credibility.

difficulties.pattern: Concession with no counter, leaving the writer's position unclear.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'It could be argued that X.' followed by a new topic; markers unsure what the writer thinks.
difficulties.response: Teach concession as a two-part move and check that every concession is followed by a response.

diagnostic.task: The learner responds in two sentences to the objection 'Online learning reduces social interaction' in an essay arguing for expanded online provision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Concedes the point accurately and limits it (While online learning can reduce informal interaction, well-designed collaborative tasks can…), with correct grammar.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Concedes but the counter merely contradicts, or there is a grammatical slip such as although…but.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ignores or dismisses the objection without engaging with it.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce concession in argumentative and discussion essays. Undergraduate in-sessional support applies it to disciplinary argument. Taught postgraduate writers use it to handle competing positions in literature reviews and to discuss limitations.

guidance.summary: Martin and White's engagement system models how texts acknowledge or suppress alternative voices. Chang and Schleppegrell made these resources explicit for L2 social-science writers and argue that explicit metalanguage helps advanced learners take effective stances; Lancaster found that higher-graded upper-level student papers more often combined acknowledging and countering alternative views. Introduce a reduced metalanguage ('opening up' and 'closing down' the discussion) before the full system, and analyse disciplinary exemplars rather than invented sentences.

activities.title: Open or close?
learnerActions: Label each clause of an exemplar paragraph as opening up or closing down the discussion
Trace the sequence across the paragraph
Explain how the sequence leads the reader to the writer's conclusion
activities.intendedInsight: Persuasive academic paragraphs often open the dialogue before narrowing it towards the writer's position.
activities.rationale: Chang and Schleppegrell's work shows the value of making engagement resources explicit for L2 writers using authentic disciplinary texts.

activities.title: Rewriting bare assertion
learnerActions: Take a paragraph of your own that consists mostly of unqualified statements
Add moves that acknowledge an alternative view or attribute a position
Close the paragraph with a contracting move that states your position
activities.intendedInsight: Acknowledging alternatives and then countering them can make a position more persuasive than bare assertion.
activities.rationale: Lancaster's comparison of higher- and lower-graded papers suggests readers in the disciplines value this pattern.

difficulties.pattern: 'Stating my opinion directly is enough to show I have a position.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of bare assertions that ignore known debates; feedback such as 'engage with the literature'.
difficulties.response: Show how expert writers position claims relative to others and practise attributing and countering specific views.

difficulties.pattern: Opening the dialogue but never closing it: balanced texts that do not conclude.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discussions that list views with equal weight and end without a position.
difficulties.response: Show that contracting moves (countering, pronouncing) are needed to state a position; practise the final move of a paragraph.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains the difference in stance between 'Some researchers claim that X' and 'Research has shown that X', and writes a sentence that acknowledges X but limits it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the first distances the writer and the second endorses, and writes an acknowledging-then-limiting sentence with appropriate resources.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Senses a difference in certainty but cannot relate it to the writer's position.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Sees the sentences as equivalent.

guidance.contextNotes: Undergraduate in-sessional work can introduce the reduced metalanguage in upper-level assignments. Taught postgraduate support applies it to literature reviews and discussion sections. Doctoral writers benefit from the full system when positioning their work in articles and theses.
reviewNotes: Lancaster (2014) studied a limited set of disciplines and assignments; the association between concede-and-counter patterns and grades should not be generalised to all fields without caution.

guidance.summary: Hyland's analysis of book reviews shows that academic criticism is typically mitigated, for example through praise–criticism pairs, hedging and specific rather than global targets. Thompson and Ye's analysis of evaluation in reporting verbs, and Petrić's finding that higher-rated master's theses used citations more for functions beyond simple attribution, point to evaluation as a marker of quality. Feak and Swales's literature-review materials provide graduate-level models. Teach critique through genre exemplars and practise varying the strength of evaluation for different readers.

activities.title: Anatomy of praise and criticism
learnerActions: Identify praise and criticism in extracts from published book reviews
Note how criticism is softened (pairing, hedging, specific target)
Write a praise–criticism pair about a text you have read this week
activities.intendedInsight: Academic criticism is usually specific and mitigated, and often paired with acknowledgement of strengths.
activities.rationale: Hyland's analysis of book reviews documents these interactional strategies in expert practice.

activities.title: Strength dial
learnerActions: Write the same critique of a study at three strengths
Decide which version suits a literature review, a critique assignment and a peer review report
Justify your choices to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: The appropriate strength of critique depends on genre, audience and the writer's purpose.
activities.rationale: Thompson and Ye's account of evaluative reporting and Feak and Swales's literature-review guidance support teaching evaluation as graded choice.

difficulties.pattern: 'Who am I to criticise a published professor?'
difficulties.revealedBy: Literature reviews that summarise without evaluation; feedback asking for critical engagement.
difficulties.response: Show that critique is an expected scholarly practice and model respectful evaluative language; start with evaluating the fit of a study to the learner's own question. This hesitation is common among novice writers of every background, including first-language English undergraduates, so do not treat it as a marker of particular educational systems.

difficulties.pattern: 'This study is wrong and useless.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Global, unmitigated evaluations without reasons or specific targets.
difficulties.response: Ask what exactly is weak and why, and rebuild the critique with a specific target, a reason and appropriate mitigation.

difficulties.pattern: Listing what studies did as if this were evaluation.
difficulties.revealedBy: Paragraphs of 'X studied… Y found… Z examined…' with no judgement of relevance or quality.
difficulties.response: Return to evaluation criteria and practise adding a judgement to each report.

diagnostic.task: The learner reads a 100-word summary of a study with a small, convenience sample and writes one evaluative sentence for a literature review.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces a specific, mitigated critique that acknowledges a contribution and names the sampling limitation and its consequence for generalisation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Names the limitation but in global or unmitigated terms, or acknowledges the study without critiquing it.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Summarises the study without evaluation.

guidance.contextNotes: Postgraduate pre-sessional courses introduce critique of single articles. Undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on evaluating sources in assignments. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers need graded evaluation for literature reviews, gap statements and peer review.

guidance.summary: Ivanič's account of writer identity (autobiographical self, discoursal self, self as author) frames voice as constructed in and through discourse. Hyland's research on authorial identity found that student writers often avoid authoritative roles, and Wingate identifies the writer's position and its relation to others' views as core components of argument that many students do not grasp. Teaching should make the linguistic resources of voice visible while respecting that adopting a new academic voice involves negotiating identity.

activities.title: Whose paragraph is it?
learnerActions: Compare two paragraphs that use the same sources: one led by the sources, one led by the writer's claim
Identify the features that make the writer visible in the second
Revise a source-led paragraph of your own to be claim-led
activities.intendedInsight: Voice is created by structure and stance choices, not only by using 'I'.
activities.rationale: Wingate's analysis of what students miss about argument points to the writer's position as the organising principle of source-based paragraphs.

activities.title: Voice reflection
learnerActions: Compare your voice in an earlier text (in any language) with your current academic draft
Note what feels comfortable and what feels borrowed
Set one specific change to try in your next draft
activities.intendedInsight: Academic voice develops through deliberate choices that can draw on, rather than erase, existing identities.
activities.rationale: Ivanič's account of the discoursal self supports reflective work on identity alongside linguistic analysis.

difficulties.pattern: 'Having a voice means writing I think.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Opinion statements added to otherwise source-led paragraphs; voice equated with personal opinion.
difficulties.response: Show the range of resources that construct voice (evaluation, framing of sources, structure) and analyse texts with strong voice and little self-mention.

difficulties.pattern: 'When I write academically, it doesn't feel like me.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Reluctance to adopt academic stance features; heavy reliance on source wording.
difficulties.response: Acknowledge identity negotiation as normal, discuss voice as a repertoire that can be extended, and avoid deficit framings of the learner's other writing.

difficulties.pattern: Paragraphs structured as a sequence of source summaries.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Smith says… Jones says… Brown says…' with the writer's view, if present, only at the end.
difficulties.response: Teach claim-led paragraph openings and the explicit marking of the writer's comment on each source.

diagnostic.task: The learner explains what a tutor means by the comment 'Where is your voice?' on a source-heavy paragraph, and proposes a revision.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Explains that the writer's own position and evaluation are not visible, and proposes a claim-led opening, evaluative framing of sources and a concluding comment.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Suggests adding 'I think' or a personal opinion without restructuring.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Interprets the comment as being about speaking or grammar.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses introduce voice through source-based paragraphs. Undergraduate in-sessional support responds to feedback about voice and criticality. Taught postgraduate and doctoral writers work on voice in literature reviews and discussions, and on identity as emerging researchers.

guidance.summary: Hyland's model treats code glosses as interactive metadiscourse through which writers anticipate readers' needs, and his study of exemplifying and reformulating shows that these markers vary by discipline. Teach code glosses as reader-oriented decisions — what does this reader need clarified? — together with the precise differences between i.e., e.g., namely and such as.

activities.title: Reader swap
learnerActions: Take a paragraph written for experts in your field
Add glosses for a non-specialist reader, then remove those an expert would not need
Compare the two versions with a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Glossing decisions depend on the intended reader.
activities.rationale: Hyland's account of code glosses as anticipating readers' knowledge supports practising adjustment for different readerships.

activities.title: i.e. or e.g.?
learnerActions: Correct sentences that confuse i.e. and e.g. or namely and such as
Check usage in authentic examples
Write one sentence of each type about your own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Reformulation specifies or restates; exemplification gives non-exhaustive instances.
activities.rationale: Hyland distinguishes reformulation from exemplification as functions of code glosses, which this contrast targets.

difficulties.pattern: 'The study used three methods, i.e. interviews' where the list is incomplete.
difficulties.revealedBy: i.e. and e.g. used interchangeably; namely used before partial lists.
difficulties.response: Contrast the abbreviations by meaning (that is versus for example) with minimal pairs.

difficulties.pattern: 'In other words' followed by a different claim.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reformulations that strengthen, narrow or change the original statement.
difficulties.response: Ask learners to check that the reformulation could replace the original without changing its meaning.

difficulties.pattern: Glossing basic field terms for an expert reader.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dissertations that define terms every reader in the field would know, while leaving novel terms unexplained.
difficulties.response: Return to the intended reader and decide which terms need glossing for that reader.

diagnostic.task: The learner adds one reformulation and one example to: 'The intervention targeted metacognitive strategies.'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Adds an accurate reformulation (that is, strategies for planning and monitoring learning) and an example with correct marker and punctuation.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Adds suitable content but confuses i.e. and e.g. or punctuates incorrectly.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Repeats the sentence or adds unrelated information.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, focus on accurate exemplification and the basic abbreviations. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional courses add reformulation and reader-oriented decisions. Taught postgraduate writers adapt glossing to expert and mixed readerships, for example in interdisciplinary dissertations.
reviewNotes: hyland2007gloss is a proposed reference; the core claims are also supported by hyland2005metadiscourse.

guidance.summary: Biber's analysis of university registers shows that stance is expressed more densely, and through different devices, in spoken registers such as classroom teaching than in academic writing. Basturkmen's work on seminar discussion shows that ideas are negotiated over several turns, so stance is often co-constructed rather than delivered as a single opinion. Teach spoken stance through recorded authentic or semi-authentic interaction, attending to prosody and turn sequences, not phrase lists alone.

activities.title: Stance in the transcript
learnerActions: Read and listen to a seminar extract
Highlight every expression of opinion, agreement, disagreement or doubt
Note how participants soften disagreement and build on each other's positions over several turns
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken stance is negotiated across turns and is often softened through hedging and vague language.
activities.rationale: Basturkmen's analysis of seminar discussion shows that meanings are negotiated collaboratively rather than stated once.

activities.title: Disagree three ways
learnerActions: Respond to a contestable statement with mild, moderate and strong disagreement
Record your responses and listen for intonation as well as words
Decide which response suits a peer seminar, a supervision and a conference question session
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken stance combines word choice and prosody, and its appropriate strength depends on the setting.
activities.rationale: Biber's evidence that spoken university registers rely heavily on stance expressions supports explicit practice of spoken stance resources.

difficulties.pattern: Avoiding disagreement in seminars, or using only 'I think'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Silence or agreement in discussion despite reservations; a narrow range of opinion frames.
difficulties.response: Provide low-stakes rehearsal of mitigated disagreement and discuss seminar expectations; do not treat reticence as a lack of ideas.

difficulties.pattern: Using written hedges in speech: 'It may be suggested that this is not correct.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Spoken contributions that sound read aloud or overly formal.
difficulties.response: Contrast spoken and written stance resources with transcripts and model natural spoken alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: Missing a lecturer's sceptical or ironic stance.
difficulties.revealedBy: Notes that record a view the lecturer was signalling doubt about; confusion when the lecturer later rejects it.
difficulties.response: Recognising irony and scepticism from the voice is demanding for most L2 listeners and depends on cultural familiarity; focused listening to prosodic stance cues helps, particularly for listeners whose other languages carry such meanings mainly through particles or word choice.

diagnostic.task: In a short role-play, the learner disagrees with a peer's interpretation of a reading and states an alternative.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses a mitigated but clear disagreement frame, gives a reason and states an alternative position, with appropriate prosody.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Disagrees clearly but bluntly, or mitigates so heavily that the position is unclear.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not express disagreement or relies on a single frame.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional courses build a basic repertoire for seminars and presentations. Undergraduate and taught postgraduate in-sessional work focuses on assessed discussion and group work. Doctoral learners need stance resources for supervisions, conference questions and the viva.

authorNotes: coh.signalling-nouns overlaps voc.abstract-shell-nouns and grm.reference-pronouns (both mention 'this + summarising noun'). I treat voc.abstract-shell-nouns as the lexical prerequisite and grm.reference-pronouns as the grammatical prerequisite; VOC and GRM authors should not make either depend on coh.signalling-nouns, or a cycle will form.

coh.connector-precision and coh.linking-adverbials overlap grm.linking-adverbial-placement and phr.bundles-text-oriented. I deliberately did not use grm.linking-adverbial-placement as a prerequisite, because placement presupposes knowing the connectors; I suggest grm.linking-adverbial-placement depend on coh.linking-adverbials.

coh.given-new depends softly on grm.passive-voice. If the GRM author makes grm.passive-voice depend on coh.given-new (function of the passive), one direction must be dropped at integration; I suggest keeping form before function as here.

Gap: Hyland's interactive categories of endophoric markers ('see Section 3', 'as noted above') and evidentials have no topic. They are partly covered by coh.frame-markers and dat.referring-to-visuals; consider broadening coh.frame-markers' scope or adding a topic.

coh.text-patterns and fun.problem-solution overlap (situation–problem–response–evaluation appears in both scope notes). I scope coh.text-patterns as recognising and using the family of patterns as reader expectations, and fun.problem-solution as the problem–solution function and its language; the edge fun.problem-solution ← coh.text-patterns encodes this.

coh.spoken-signposting overlaps lis.lecture-discourse-markers and prs.signposting. I authored it as the shared linguistic resource; I suggest lis.lecture-discourse-markers and prs.signposting take it as a prerequisite rather than the reverse.

coh.writer-responsibility: Hinds's typology is contested. Consider renaming the topic 'Explicitness and reader expectations' so the taxonomy does not appear to endorse a national typology. I suggest idn.intercultural-rhetoric depend on this topic rather than the reverse.

Cycle-risk edges to check at integration: coh.paragraph-transitions ← par.topic-sentences and coh.writer-responsibility ← wpr.audience-purpose assume the PAR/WPR topics are more foundational. I removed earlier edges from par.paragraph-unit and ess.essay-structure because, in other groups' current parts, those topics sit downstream of coh.linking-adverbials and sta.hedging (par.paragraph-unit ← rds.main-ideas ← rds.paragraph-structure-reading ← coh.linking-adverbials). Making the concept of a paragraph depend on reading topics and connectors looks inverted and may be worth reviewing.

fun.describing-process overlaps dat.describing-diagrams; fun.hypothesising overlaps dse.hypothesis-language. The DSE and DAT authors appear to have made their topics depend on the FUN topics, which matches my intended direction.

Several FUN topics start at B1 while some grammar and vocabulary prerequisites authored by other groups start at B1+ or B2 (for example voc.evaluative-lexis B2, grm.non-finite-clauses B2, grm.nominalisation B2). I dropped those edges instead of raising the functions' entry levels, since foundation learners meet these functions early; the more advanced realisations (nominalised causation, precise evaluative lexis) remain in the mastery statements.

fun.summarising-concluding overlaps src.summarising-passage, src.summarising-text and ess.conclusions. I scope it as summarising and concluding from the writer's own content; I suggest ess.conclusions depend on it.
fun.recommending and fun.problem-solution overlap grp.business-report and grp.case-study; I suggest those genres depend on these functions.

fun.evaluating and sta.evaluating-others-language overlap. I scope fun.evaluating as general criterion-based evaluation and sta.evaluating-others-language as its application to other scholars' work, linked by sta.evaluating-others-language ← fun.evaluating.
fun.evaluating depends softly on crt.description-analysis-evaluation; the CRT author should not make that topic depend on fun.evaluating.

crt.description-analysis-evaluation currently depends on fun.explaining (CRT part), and fun.evaluating depends on it; this is acyclic, but the CRT author should not add an edge from fun.evaluating or fun.problem-solution.

sta.metadiscourse is modelled as a synthesising concept learnt after learners have met frame markers and hedging, so it is not a prerequisite of sta.hedging or sta.boosters. If other strands treat it as an entry-point concept, the direction of these edges should be reconsidered.

sta.generalisation-qualification overlaps reg.vague-overgeneralised, num.approximation and the approximator subtype of sta.hedging.
